review_text: I booked the 2 day Santiago city tour with City Trekking Tours for two based on the reviews posted on Trip Advisor. Ignacio (Nacho) arrived at our hotel at the appointed time and he happily agreed, with no notice, for us to add a third member to our group at the tour rate. We initially headed off towards Barrio Bellavista where we walked through Patio Bellavista and onto Pablo Neruda’s house (which we visited later on) and then to Cerro San Cristobal. The tour went on to cover the fruit and vegetable market, the fish market and then landmarks in the centre of town including the Plaza de Armas, the Presidential Palace and much, much more. We could have climbed Cerro Santa Lucia but having done so the day before decided to omit this. We stopped for a late lunch in Barrio Lastarria and then headed back to our hotel via Gabriela Mistral Cultural Centre. It was a lot of walking but Nacho would have slowed the pace had we asked. On the second day we went to Sky Costanera, the tallest building in South America, to take in the views of Santiago. As the visibility was very poor Nacho offered to deduct the cost of going up the building from the cost of the tour so that we could go back another day. We decided to go up anyway and ended up having the best view of Santiago covered in fog!! We then walked around this part of town ending at Los Dominicos artisan village with a tasty empanada and a look at the shops. The 2 day tour was perfect for sampling what Santiago has to offer so you could go back and explore on your own. Having had such a great time with Nacho, we decided we wanted to book more. We went on to book three further tours: A day tour to Valparaiso We started with a visit to Pablo Neruda’s eclectic house, La Sebastiana, following which Nacho had arranged us to be guided by Felipe around this UNESCO designated town. The tour incorporated the breathtakingly beautiful murals, a brief history of the town, lunch and a walk around the port. Horse riding in the mountains We saddled up and headed off into the mountains on this slow paced horse ride. You could lose yourself in the magnificent scenery until you head back to a tasty barbecue. Wine tour to Concha y Toro followed by a visit to Cajon del Maipo An interesting visit to this iconic winery included 3 wine tastings which was quite a feat as they were all completed before 11am! We then headed to Cajon del Maipo for an icy walk to get more fabulous views. Having only a pair of low heeled, fashion boots I was concerned about slipping only to find the rest of my group, with far more appropriate footwear, sliding and falling all over the place providing me with plenty of light entertainment!! I highly recommend the walk in the Chilean winter as the views at our destination with snow capped mountains were amazing and well worth the walk. All in all we had a great time with Nacho who felt more like a friend than a guide. If you want a private tour, I would have no hesitation in recommending this company as each tour was efficiently organized and most enjoyable. If you find yourself in Santiago for a short stay I recommend the first day of the city tour (try and include Pablo Neruda’s house) followed by the day trip to Valparaiso. Dear Carina, Thank you very much for having chosen us! I'm glad that you liked the tours through Santiago, Valparaíso and the mountains. I really happy that I have met you: D! You and your family are the kind of people that I will never forget! You are so motivated, easygoing, trustful and happy that it will be always a pleasure to share with you! I had so much fun with you and I learnt a lot from you, molly and Toby. We were lucky that we had a good weather and that you were able to appreciate all the places at its maximum =) When I had to say you “See you later” I felt I was saying it to very good friends! So, I now that I will see you again in the future! … Who knows where! Whenever you come back just let me know and i will more than happy to show you around again, this time as a friend =)! Continue enjoying the life and travelling the world! We'll keep in touch Nacho

review_text: Seven of us were picked up from our hotel in Santiago in a van by Felipe and Diego, our guides. They were very passionate about nature, their job, Chile and the mountains. We made a breakfast stop whilst they collected supplies for the trip, and then we continued beyond Cajón del Maipo to the volcanos. There we got off and Diego took us on a fairly easy hike with absolutely breathtaking views of the Andes. We ranged from 20-60 in age and were all happy. After about 2 km stopped, had a picnic and some time to connect with nature and then came down again, to be taken to the hot springs. This place is rustic and unspoiled. I would recommend taking a towel and flip flops (I forgot both!) but if felt amazing in the hot water with the stunning views. When we were ready to leave, they took us back to the place where we had had breakfast for some tapas and a drink. All was included except for breakfast. We had a great time, enjoyed listening to Diego and Felipe, and have memories for a life time. Hopefully will be back for more adventures

review_text: This was my first winery tour and I wasn't disappointed. We had the English tour booked for us and it turns out, we were the only ones that picked the timeslot, so we got a private tour. My friend has been to wineries in California and South Africa and we both had fun on the tour. It was great to walk around the rows and rows of grapes and pick out some to taste. Our guide was really knowledgeable about the grape varieties and answered any silly question we had about them and the wine making process. It was fun to see the little garden with all the grape varieties that we can try and compare taste/sugar levels from. The underground cellar was the best part of the tour and since we were such a small group, we got to see more than the larger groups would have. My favorite was definitely seeing the giant vats that were used years ago. We tasted four varieties at the end and I really enjoyed tasting the TH line. I wish it was easier to buy the Undurraga wine in the US so I can re-live the experience!

review_text: We wanted to see the Pacific during our trip to Santiago. We booked about 3 weeks before departing for Chile. The online booking was simple and straightforward through Trip Advisor and Viator. Gabriel (Gabe) was our guide for the day. He picked us up from our hotel promptly at the agreed upon time from emails with Alexandra and set off in his van with another couple. On the way, he shared with us some interesting facts about the region. His English was great. We made a stop at a vineyard, Veramonte where we tasted some great local wines and learned some history about their unique production methodologies. Onward to Vina del Mar. The city was lovely with a beachy feel and colourful houses. We drove up and down the beach to see the walruses and visit the local Easter Island relic and main Plaza in the downtown. We then stopped for lunch at the Castillo del Mar restaurant. A little bit pricey, but this restaurant had excellent food and excellent views of the ocean. After lunch Gabe came to meet us and we travelled onwards to Valparaiso. Again colourful houses with lots of artistic graffiti gave the town a bohemian beachy vibe. We drove all around Valparaiso, up and down the narrow roadways. We stopped at the Nuredo house for a great view of the city and coastline. Then we stopped at an excellent viewpoint of the working, busy port, it was interesting to watch the all of the cargo containers moving around. Some small souvenir shops were here as well. When we were done, the drive back to Santiago was uneventful and quick. I must admit I fell asleep in the van as the day had been so chock full of sight-seeing and we had such a great time. The group was very small, only one other couple so it was a very intimate and personal tour, which was exactly what we were looking for. While it might have been possible to arrange all of these things as well as transportation on our own, the packaging of the winery and trip to the coast all into one package was fantastic since it was all done in one day and we were able to make the most or our time on our short stay in Santiago. We would highly recommend this tour to any travellers looking into this since it is such a nice package covering different things in one day with a knowledgeable and friendly host.

review_text: The trip out to the island takes about 90 minutes and while we had good seas I can imagine it would be challenging for those with motion sickness if the weather wasn't great. to get off the boat on the island you walk down a steep metal gangway from the boat directly onto the shore. the path is packed direct and has stones throughout so you need to be mindful of this when walking the path. the route is one way about a mile and requires you to climb a hill that gets quite steep towards the middle near the lighthouse. The volume of penguins is significant and you can see that they are comfortable with people as they will walk right across your path without hesitation. You can see them in the water, on land and in their burrows easily. It's well worth the visit and I recommend this to any penguin lover.

review_text: After backpacking through Torres del Paine, me and a buddy were up in Pucon looking for more adventure. We were lucky to find Montanas del Sur. Like another poster said, it feels like you're just traveling with friends, not a strict and cookie-cutter guided tour. For the Volcan Villarica hike, all our gear was provided. The views from the top were incredible and being able to say you hiked the most active volcano in South America (which last erupted like 8 years ago) is pretty cool. After reaching the top, instead of just hiking back down, you use these little sleds to slide down -- unbelievably fun. This hike was definitely more fun than we expected and a major highlight of our weeks in Chile. We also went on a tour with Montanas del Sur to Termas Geometricas, a super cool nearby hot springs. Finally, the Montanas guys were very helpful with recommendations for local restaurants, places to visit, shops to stop by, everything. We are so lucky to have found this awesome group! Review of: Full Day Mountaineering to Villarrica Volcano from Pucón

review_text: One of South America's largest cemeteries with over 2 million buried here, the General Cemetery is large indeed--so bring a good pair of walking shoes as well as something to drink. The red line will drop you off in front of the cemetery gate, but don't enter here. Walk around the block to the front entrance for a better first view. The cemetery streets inside are lined with mausoleums, palms and rows of graves. All but two of the Chile's presidents are buried here as well as other notables. Large building too are erected to honor military and members of special social clubs and organizations. You will see everything from ornate mausoleums to graves that are quite ordinary. During the holidays family come out and really give their former family members a special treat--for ex., at Christmas they will bring Christmas trees and santas as well as tinsel strung from tree to gave.

review_text: We took the full-day trip. It was a 90 minute drive from Puerto Varas down to the Rio San Pedro near Maullin. A short boat ride over to the ranch where the horses were. After a gradual introduction to the horses, we saddled up and rode up and over the peninsula, down along the beach and back through the working ranch. Cristian was a great host and guide. The ranch owner, Pepe, was patient with our modest equestrian skills. The horses were well cared for and easy to ride. The weather was gloomy at the start but the sun came out later. The scenery was beautiful and peaceful. After the ride there was a delicious and abundant home-cooked lunch by Pepe's wife. Salmon from the sea and lamb from the ranch. All in all a great day and excellent insight into the ranching life of southern Chile.

review_text: My wife and I were in Santiago from December 22, 2016 through January 12, 2017. We were touring the Plaza de Armas and decided to tour the National Museum of History which faces the Plaza. This Museum seems to specialize in Chilean Spanish Colonial History. There were painting of Pedro Valdivia, the Spanish founder of Santiago. It detailed the history of fighting the fierce Indians in Chile and explained how Valdivia, then the governor of Chile, died in one of the battles with the Indians. It also had paintings of captured Indians including one of the captures of one of the major chiefs of the fierce Indians who did not want the Spanish in their territory. It also had a room devoted to the Spanish Colonial society with dresses, tools, kitchen equipment, societal balls and some history regarding the daily life in the Colonial society. It was a interesting and fascinating experience even though everything was in Spanish. I don't exactly recall the admission price although my memory is that it was most reasonable. I recommend that any tourist should visit this museum to get an idea of the history of the early Spanish Colonial period in Chilean history.

review_text: Tour that is usually done in conjunction with the Altiplanicas Lagunas. Also known as Salar de Aguas Calientes or Salar de Talar, it is 150 km from San Pedro de Atacama and at 4,200m altitude. We got a cold wind – the temperature was 6°, but the thermal sensation should be below zero. It's one of those places where you're not tired of taking pictures and admiring. The red stones of the name are formed by volcanic lava with high iron content which, in contact with lower temperature, solidifies. When the iron is exposed to air, it ends up oxidizing, giving it a red rust color. In my opinion, together with the Altiplanicas Lagunas, it is the best walk from San Pedro de Atacama.

review_text: My friend and I thoroughly enjoyed the 4 day kayaking trip in the Northern Patagonia Fjords. What stuck out on this trip was how unique an experience it is. You paddle in amazing fjords, learn about the life of local fishing families and experience their simple but inspiring culture. I think Juanfe has set up a great balance of enjoyment from paddling and local interaction. On other guided trips you often do not get to interact so closely with the locals. On this trip, we ate a delicious dinner every night in a local family's home and camped near their home. If you are looking for a unique outdoors experience, this trip is a great fit. Juanfe is a good guide that tries to balance schedule, weather and the happiness of his clients. Reading some past reviews, I can see where some of their opinions can be valid, but I think it depends on your expectations. To be concise and open, here is what I considered to be the highlights and areas of improvement of the trip: Highlights: - local interactions: eating and interacting with local families was a lovely experience I wasn't expecting - scenery: jaw dropping fjord scenery and wildlife (dolphins, penguins and king fishers) - safety: Juanfe was always clear about safety first and let us know about things to take caution of - education: Juanfe makes a good effort to teach you about paddling techniques, culture and history - off-the-grid: You will not see another tourist on the water. It is a great reminder of how the simple life, is a great life. Areas of improvement: - reading other reviews, there were mentions of female clients receiving different treatment. My friend was female and she was treated with equal respect. Having said that, there were moments where I noticed other females were treated with less patience and flexibility. - communication style: Most of the instructions Juan gave were clear. There were a few instances where he would say one thing but mean another, and I would suspect that it was because English is not Juan's first language. For example: one time he said to meet at 7pm for dinner, but what he meant was meet no later than 7pm, so he expected us earlier than that. So we found it was best to clarify about important things with him. Bottomline: If you are looking for a fun and unique experience, I would highly recommend this trip. review_text: We just returned from a fantastic trip with this company. The group consisted of ten seasoned travelers who are experienced cyclists. We chose an aggressive itinerary averaging over 60 miles daily on hilly terrain. We exceeded 80mi on two days. The Tour consisted of one week of cycling beginning in Temuco, Chile. We cycled around Lake Villarica in Pucon, then climbed the Andes crossing into Argentina. Once in Argentina we cycled from Junin de los Andes to San Martin, around the Seven Lakes region, then back across the Andes down to Puyuhe, Chile. The trip in Chile took us to Puerto Octay, then Puerto Varas, and finished with a grueling climb up the Osorno Volcano. Ecotours provided excellent guides and sag wagon support. Our guides included professional cyclists who provided coaching as well as directional support. Most of us brought our own bikes, three of us rented perfectly adequate Trek bikes. The two sag vehicles were never more than ten minutes away from the group, but were never intrusive. We had one flat over the trip and the sag wagon showed up in less than two minutes with assistance. Overall, we stayed at excellent hotels and dined at fabulous restaurants. The Spa at Puyuhue, surprisingly a five star hotel, and the hotel at Puerto Octay were not as satisfactory as the others. The Villarica Park Hotel, the Sol Arrayan, the 3-star Hostel at Junin, and the Hotel Patagonico at Puerto Varas were superb. Ecotour arranged three dinners and we chose the rest. I would strongly recommend this outfit to anyone considering cycling in Chile and Argentina. I would advise that cycling in Chile and Argentina is more about the terrain, nature, fantastic scenery, and great people. Food quality in restaurants was superb. Unlike along many cycling routes in France, Spain, or Italy, there is not a fancy restaurant with a wine bar and an espresso machine every ten miles. We cycled mostly through undeveloped and unspoiled national parks. The picnic lunches provided were well planned with good local food and were well situated relative to the cycling.

review_text: I first discovered Casa Marin on a list of "world's best winery hotels". Little did I know that, when we left the Colchagua Valley (the "best" wine region in Chile, according to conventional wisdom) to take the 3 hour drive north-west to Lo Abarca, we'd be stumbling on to the biggest (and most delightful) surprise of our trip: the wine at Casa Marin was, hands down, our favourite wine in Chile. It may even have been our favourite wine in South America. The secret comes from the particularly mineral-rich soil in Lo Abarca, and from the daily temperature fluctuations, both caused by the valley's proximity to the Pacific Ocean. The wines are crisp, rich, flavourful, and unique - one sip of the one-of-a-kind sauvignon blanc (with a hint of asparagus (!!) on the nose) is reason enough to visit. We didn't end up staying at the hotel (a gorgeous cottage up a hill that has a view of the ocean), because the previous night's rain had rendered the road up to the cottage entirely impassable. Not to be outdone by Mother Nature, the incredibly generous people at Casa Marin arranged a room for us at the frankly stunning "Winery Boutique Hotel" about 30 minutes north of Lo Abarca in Algarrobo. The balcony was almost literally perched right over the Pacific Ocean. The list of superlatives in the English language is not sufficient to express how excited we are that we discovered Casa Marin; we'll definitely be paying another visit in the not-too-distant future.

review_text: Take a guided tour through the villa and learn all about the history of the torture that occurred here and realize that the Chileans have a different concept of memory than that compared to Europe, and the Holocaust. It is a peaceful park with flowers representing women victims, mosaic signs on the ground representing how victims were blindfolded and could only see parts of the ground, and has a replica of an isolation cell with drawings of prisoners' experiences inside. Tour of a replica of the tower where many victims met their end, as well as the "changing rooms," an original tiny building which now holds personal effects of a few victims. Finally, pass the pool where the secret police's children would play while victims were tortured just across the villa. Leaving the villa, be sure to see the parts of train rails used to sink victims just off the Chilean coast.

Tour of a replica of the tower where many victims met their end, as well as the "changing rooms," an original tiny building which now holds personal effects of a few victims. Finally, pass the pool where the secret police's children would play while victims were tortured just across the villa. Leaving the villa, be sure to see the parts of train rails used to sink victims just off the Chilean coast.

review_text: For those who have always wanted to see Antarctica, but who don't want to risk a rough 3-day crossing through the Drake Passage (and we certainly didn't) flying to Antarctica is the easy way to make that trip. We started with an excellent tour briefing in the Hotel Cabo de Hornos in the town of Punta Arenas in the southern tip of Chile. This was the start point for our 6-day cruise in the Antarctic, and we flew to King George Island the next day. We flew in a comfortable aircraft taking all 67 guests, for about two hours and landed at a scientific base on Frei Island. Then we boarded small Zodiacs about ten guests at a time, and were taken to our ship, the Ocean Nova. All the arrangements and transfers of both guests and baggage were handled very professionally and efficiently. Once on the ship we were shown to our very compact and comfortable cabin, complete with two bunks and a tiny but very usable bathroom. There were 67 guests, 33 crew and 12 guides on our cruise. This vessel only operates in the few summer Antarctic months otherwise the ice becomes too dense. The emphasis on this cruise is active adventure for these who want to learn about Antarctica, its history, its geography, and especially its wildlife. We saw more penguins than we could count in different places on different days. We saw three types of seals, plenty of humpback whales, and lots of different seabirds. All were well explained to us in presentations by our expert guides after dinner, and also during the guided treks and walks. We visited several research bases, and one historic Antarctic Museum, all of which were interesting. Each evening we were briefed on the activities we could select for the next day, and in the morning after a great buffet breakfast we went ashore in the Zodiacs to do whatever we had chosen. The guides were professional and helpful, the systems were smooth and efficient, All the guests were soon doing whatever they wanted for the morning, Back to the ship for a great lunch, then in the afternoon there would be other activities ashore if you wanted to do them. Dinner was just as good – plenty of excellent food, and wine was always includes. Some of us tried snowshoeing for the first time in our lives, and learned the simple techniques to make this fun although it can be quite energetic. Others went for walks in the snow, with guides leading the way and explaining what we were seeing and experiencing. This was one of the best adventure holidays we have ever had. The company is very professional and well run, communication with guests is very well handled, and the whole process is made easy and pleasant. We would rate this a 10 out of 10 experience. The ship, the cabin, the food, the staff, the crew and the guides combine to make this a wonderful holiday, with a lot packed into a short time. Yes, it is expensive, but then having amazing 5-star experiences in a place few people are privileged to visit was worth every cent. One thing is for sure: we will remember this holiday as long as we live, and have no hesitation in recommending it to others. If you have any questions please write via Trip Advisor and we’ll be happy to assist if we can. No, we do not have any association with the company or the ship. We just had such a good time that we are happy to share it with others.

review_text: We did two trips with On Safari. The first was an astronomy lesson, led by Juan Pablo, and the second was the Machuca all day hike, led by Ignacio. The astronomy lesson was fantastic--but note that it is not advanced level. There is another company in Atacama that does much higher level astronomy lessons. I went in not particularly knowledgable about astronomy, so I really enjoyed Juan Pablo's lecture and the great stargazing we were able to do with his guidance. He also provides some drinks and snacks. It's a breezy 90m total, which is great. The hike may have been one of the best days of my life. We were skeptical about paying $240pp for a hike, but it was definitely well worth it. The hike goes from 4300m down to Rio Grande village at over 3000m, and you can see the many different changes in vegetation/wildlife/etc. At 16km and high elevation throughout, this is not a walk for the unfit. That said, it is mostly downhill and those who are in good physical condition should have no problem. We stopped for lunch at a beautiful old house before continuing the hike through the afternoon. Communication was really great before and after the trips, and payment was fairly simple via PayPal. Would highly recommend.

review_text: We used Santiago Adventures for a private bike tour of wineries in the Casablanca Valley and they were outstanding. The biking was at the perfect level for us, although I felt sure it would have been customized to those with more experience. While the price may initially seem high, once you see the level of expertise, attention and overall quality of service you realize the price:quality ratio is extremely good. Would use them again in a heartbeat.

review_text: Some of my friends had booked a day to Valparaiso/Vina del Mar and another day to tour wineries. But I was short on time, so decided to see both in one day with this tour. The tour was more expensive than some others, but it was worth it for me. I was able to see several things in one day, and I got to go with a smaller group instead of on a huge tour bus. Actually, the number of people on the tour was almost a problem. I booked the tour a couple of weeks in advance, but no one else booked it until the night before. It was almost canceled, which was stressful. I had to wait until the last minute to see if the tour would happen. This may have been because it was low season. If no one else had signed up, Itours promised to put me on a tour with another company. The guide was very nice, although he didn't give us quite as much information about the country and culture as I thought he might. We spent most of the day driving, but it wasn't bad. We had a private tour at Emiliana vineyard, which was really nice and so beautiful. We got to see alpacas, sheep, and chickens there. The guide even took me to a separate (non-tourist) area to see a new baby alpaca! We also saw the Easter Island statue and the ocean and sea lions at Vina del Mar, plus a scenic stop-off or two along the way. The beach was beautiful, and the guide allowed us plenty of time to take pictures and look out at the water. Throughout the day, he was very accommodating to what we wanted to do. This is why I like a smaller tour group like this. We ate at a restaurant in Vina del Mar which was fine. I was worried that we were going to eat at the castle, the tourist trap where most of the Vina/Valparaiso tours go. But we didn't. This place was decently priced (although most restaurants in Chile are more expensive than in the US). We then drove to and around Valparaiso. At first, the town didn't seem like anything special, but then we started seeing the beautiful houses and other buildings that make it famous. We got out once or twice, but I would have liked to look around more. The tour was timed so that we would be in Valparaiso in the evening, when the sun makes all the buildings glow golden. It was beautiful! After all that driving we were ready to head home to Santiago. I enjoyed the tour, and would recommend it if you don't mind paying a little more to see a lot in one day.

review_text: Picture this....hot sun, blue skies, white sands and turquoise waters.....now jump in! You float!!! The water was so beautiful and refreshing and fun! At the entrance, be sure to grab a couple of containers of water to wash off all the salt. There are Baños and changing rooms. Our guide, Mauricio, set up a refreshing snack while we floated and took pictures. There isn't anything available for purchase so bring your drinking water and snacks. Dont forget your camera and sunscreen. The sand is beautiful to walk on so you can easily walk barefeet. There is limited shade - if none at all. We went in the morning - which our guide told us is the least busy times. He was right - we just about had the place to ourselves. Honestly, the following day we drove to Salar de Tara and all I kept thinking of was that I wished I was back at the Laguna Cejar.

review_text: My wife and I booked two days with Tom for wine tastings at the tail end of a cruise. We collected three offers from different tour operators. Tom absolutely hit it out of the park. Small-ish wineries, great driver, great lodging and dinner reservations. Mario was our driver - busy and really nice young man and he has worked in the wine industry so he was far more than a driver. Tom set us up with Casa Marin, Tinta Tinto, Matetic, Villard, and Bodegas RE. Some highlights: Tinta Tinto is probably the most fun we ever had at a tasting. Family place - mom, dad, two very pleasant adult daughters making wine in their (very nice) backyard. The entire experience was a 10++. Matetic might have been the biggest winery of the visit and I really appreciated the tutorial on bio-dynamic wine-making. I had no idea. Matetic has a ten room hotel. I knew when we booked the trip I would want two nights there instead of just one. I could take three nights there, Really neat. The other wineries were fine with Bodegas RE probably being the best of the rest. If I were to drop one of them - Villard would fall off the list. Finished the two day visit at Vinamar for a great lunch on their balcony with wine pairings - beautiful setting. I do not want to be petty but there was one thing about working with Tom that i did not like. He is a CASH ONLY business. I'm OK with that but I started developing this wine trip three months before we got on a 17-day cruise. Tom and i had several substantive e-mail exchanges where all he had to tell was he was CASH ONLY. So, we are on a cruise ship with a busted ATM, we are in Lima during the state of emergency with no ability to do banking and I need to find about $800. This situation was easily avoided by Tom and turned out to be an inconvenience for me as it compromised my ability to leave tips for the cruise staff. The trip was still a 5 but could have been a 5+

review_text: I am a passionate animal lover and to see the size of some of these enclosures were appalling for the the size of some of the animals. The zoo has the right concept.. But it was things like having the llamas in an enclosure the lions, zebra, kangaroos, elephants or giraffes should have had. It came to our attention the whole day that some of the smaller animals were in larger enclosures then what the BIG animals were in. I was disgusted with some enclosure size to animal ratio. Also there were a lot of animal enclosures that were WAY to over populated. For example, the big porcupines had at least 10 of them in one TINY enclosure. A lot of the time the zoo stunk so bad it made me feel sick. I could go on and list every animal that had a small pen/cage/enclosure and how over populated or lonely and agitated some animals were. But I'll stop here. My advice for the zoo would be to change locations for the comfort of visitors feeling sorry for them, and to make your animals comfortable. We saw so many animals known to be hyper, playful and active that were so sedentary, that it was worrying. So as a animal lover it was hard to leave knowing they will continue to live like this and there isn't anything I can do.. I just hope something changes to help these beautiful creatures. There were some good aspects about the zoo like the weight of the animals, but to me, the bad outweigh the good unfortunately. I will show some photos of the enclosures that I thought were unacceptable. If you google Melbourne zoo Australia, that is why my standards are so high.. And so should everyone else's!!

review_text: First off the ship (as usual) on a cool, dark morning in Coquimbo, we were met by a smiling Jorge, our friendly, personable guide from Ecoturismo La Serena (http://www.ecoturismolaserena.cl/?lang=en). We had told the company exactly what we wanted to see during our limited time in port, and they had come up with a perfect itinerary. Jorge shared a wealth of information about Coquimbo, La Serena and Vicuña. We drove through a cloudy Elqui Valley and were shocked to see the effects of the drought that has plagued the area for years. In contrast, during our visit to the Aba Piscu distillery we saw evidence of the flooding and mudslides caused by the recent unseasonable torrential rains. By the end of the day, the Sun had decided to make an appearance and burn off the stubborn layer of clouds. Finally we had blue skies and were able to see the surrounding mountains, allowing us to appreciate the upper reaches of the Elqui Valley in all its glory. All in all, we had a fantastic day and would highly recommend Ecoturismo La Serena when visiting this stunning part of the world.

review_text: There are two common routes to access the El Morado National Monument Park, one access through the Quebrada Morales valley and starts near community were the Baño Morales hostel is located. This place is very close to the Camino al Vulcan road, and is the one you have pay a pass to get in. You leave the car there at the community and start the trekking right there. This trekking stars at 1840 m and goes up to 2500 near the lake and the San Franscisco Glacier viewpoint. It is considered an 5-6 hours, easy to medium hike. The other trail is located on the following valley, on the next exit to the left. This is the one you leave the car next to the mining company gate (or, if you have a SUV or truck, you can go up about 3,5 km deep on the Las arenas Valley). This trekking start much higher (2450 m - near the mining gate) and go to (3120 m - at the hanging glacier lake) and gets much colder. Depending on your condition or adaption (due to the altitude) it can be a strenuous hike, 4 hours round trip if you are fit, and around 7 if not.

review_text: So you meet in the Soto Mayer at 10am or 3pm daily and in the square you will find the guides with their distinctive red and white shirts. Based on the number of people that show up the guides divide the group between English speakers and Spanish speakers. The guides then take off with group in hand. The tour last three hours. During the 10am tour you walk downtown, then bus up the hill and walk again through several public spaces ending back in the town square where you begin. The guides moved at a good pace and essentially you get three hours to chat with the local guide who pointed out everything you can imagine about Valpo and Chile. The tour is free but folks are expected to tip the guide in the 8-10 US dollar range. This was the best thing we did in Chile. Every city should have free guided walking tours like this. I learned tons and visited places I would not have seen. The tours are different, if I had come back for the 3pm tour we would have visited learned the history of the Old Port and then visited the two most popular Cerros in Valpo (Concepcion and its neighbor).

review_text: Our familiar experience with the company Indo Pro Chile was simply impeccable! From the first contact, the team demonstrated extreme punctuality and receptivity, making the entire process of hiring, payment and access to details very easy, organized, transparent and secure. The guide Felipe was one of the great differentials of the tour: his depth of knowledge about the region, history and local culture made every moment enriching. In addition, their kindness and attention to detail made the experience even more special. We had the opportunity to meet the beaches of the Pacific, where we could appreciate the grandness of the ocean and feel the unique atmosphere of the Chilean coast, as well as understand the relationship of the Chilean to the beach (which is very different from the relationship of the Brazilian to the beach). Besides, the visit to the Pablo Neruda Museum was one of the highlights of the trip. Knowing the history and the details of the life and work of this great poet, in such an inspiring environment, made the experience culturally enriching. We made the tour to Cajón del Maipo and the thermas with our two children, 10 and 14, and we were all delighted! It was a true immersion in the Andes, with stunning landscapes and unique moments in the mountains. The experience of relaxing in the thermal waters surrounded by such an impressive setting was unforgettable for the whole family. The Aylan Winehouse and the sunset was a romantic moment, which my husband and I liked very much. And before that, Felipe allowed us to make a tasting at the Concha Y Toro winery, which was not included in the tour, for purely kindness. By the way, kindness is what is not missing, we were very well received, treated and in the end we still won a ride to the airport! Beyond amazing landscapes, we had the opportunity to experience local cuisine and get to know the region’s crafts, which made the experience even more authentic and enriching. The safe driving (with details of altitude, location, temperature, humidity and other very interesting data for those who visit Chile – Felipe has it all at hand or in his mind), the well planned roadmap and the care of the team allowed us to take advantage of every moment to the fullest, ensuring comfort and fun for everyone. Our children loved every moment, which made the trip even more special. If you are looking for a complete, authentic and well-organized experience in Chile, I recommend Indo Pro Chile without hesitation! review_text: If you have one day or twenty days in Santiago, start with this tip-based walking tour of the city. Franco, a musician at an Irish pub in Bellavista by night, is also a talented and engaging tour guide by day. His 4 hour tour brought this city, its history and its culture to life for our band of English speaking visitors. It is a leisurely and entertaining walk around the key cultural, historical and social sites of Santiago, and provided us with a sense of the city's turbulent history from pre-Columbian times to the troubles of the Pinochet era. The tour finale was the Bellavista neighbourhood and the home of Pablo Neruda. Each location was outlined with great humour and insight. Four hours may seem a long time, but it was nicely divided by a relaxed lunch break in the hip Lastarria neighbourhood. And it was over too quickly. Given the rarity of rain in Santiago and the flexibility of booking these tours, it is a must for visitors. Franco's tour gave us a great taste of the city, and left us a long list of places to visit.

review_text: Don't let the 3 stars throw you off that this isn't a nice destination visit when in Santiago. This park is huge with lots to do from hiking up el Cerro San Cristobal, picnicing, to the zoo. Cerro San Cristobal has the most stunning panoramic views of the city and the Andes in Santiago! We were able to captivate some wonderful drone shots!The Virgin Mary statue is a peaceful sanctuary for those who seek prayer. However, although el Parque Metropolitano is absolutely beautiful, it lacks to be tourist friendly. Ensure you take cash, because to enter the park you need to pay either per person or vehicle and there are is no ATM nor bank nearby. We circled an hour (because parking in front of a bank is non-existent in Santiago) to find a place to take out money. Before visiting el Parque Metropolitano, I checked the website to ensure that the teleférico was operating because when I had gone in the past, the teleférico had been closed and in repair due to the earth quake of 2010. It finally opened in early 2017 so I thought "YES" the teleférico is open and I can finally go. Although the website said that the teleférico operated Tuesday - Sunday when I went on a Tuesday it was closed for regular maintenance... This really ticked me off because on the website it said that the maintenance days were Monday's not Tuesday's. In the past, there used to be a way to drive all the way up to the Virgin Mary (the first two times we drove straight up the cerro). Parking is very limited so if you get lucky you'll find a spot. However, when i just went we were obligated to hike 8KM round trip (up and down the cerro) to see the Virgin. This was challenging since we were with our 11 month old who doesn't walk yet but at least we had our stroller. Once we got to the resting area close to the Virgin after about 45 minutes of walking up hill, the elevators to get to the Virgin were not working so we had to hike up the stairs with our stroller to see the Virgin! Although this is one of the top tourist destinations of Santiago, it definitely lacks to be tourist friendly! Yes the park is beautiful, but it is poorly managed for tourists.

review_text: We had an amazing time visiting the glacier with Waeskar expeditions. It's a long boat ride to the glacier but the boat is cozy, there's an inside where you can stay warm and an outside where you can sit and enjoy the amazing views and take pictures. Our guide Sebastian (who speaks French, Spanish, and English) was lovely and knowledgeable about the area and also really funny. The captain Sylvia is super professional and navigated us through the ice field like a pro. We got to land near the glacier, maybe half a kilometer away, and climb all over taking cool pictures. I was really impressed by the level of customer service--the group was small so I felt like we got a lot of attention from the staff. They cook lunch for you on the boat--ours was soup and risotto--and they even provided a vegetarian option. After lunch we went exploring for a while longer and enjoyed pisco sours while looking out at the glacier, which was a really unique experience. They even provided a snack on the way back. I highly recommend this tour, it's a long day but a truly unique experience.

review_text: Can't recommend this company enough. We were due to do the W-Trek in March 2020 which we had to cancel after we arrived in Puerto Natales due to covid park closures. Ricci was super helpful, letting us stay in the cabins, and helping us to organise a way to get home as our travel plans all got cancelled. He also agreed to hold our tickets for us, and said we were welcome back whenever we could make it. Flash forward to October 2022 and we finally had the chance to come back and do it. Firstly, you will receive the warmest of welcomes, with an airport pick up, as much food and drink (more on that in a moment) as you can manage, and a stay in the comfortable garden domes or lodges. The communication, organisation, and booking process is exceptional, and the team go above and beyond to accommodate all requests and amendments. Ricci, Gonzo, and the team are wonderful hosts. Ricci's passion for Patagonia is infectious and he makes a real effort to get to know every single guest he has. He is also a "foodie" and has hired an exceptional chef Claudio (Ex-Singular) to prepare incredible food pre and post trek (make sure to try the brisket pizza). Your tea cup and wine glass will never be empty. You have a day/night to relax at the property before you head in to the park, at which point you will get all the information and direction you need for the next 4 days. Note that we did the W Trek Active and it was well worth the wait! The first day of the hike (to the base of the towers) is accompanied by 2 professional guides, who provide support, tips and information to ensure you get the most out of your time in the park. There is one clear route which is clearly signposted throughout, so even for the more directionally challenged it is pretty hard to go wrong. After the first day with the guides, you are required to complete the rest of the hike on your own, at your own pace although you will have a group around you should you need support. We had a great group of hikers, all at different fitness and experience levels, so most often we all set off together but then met up at the rest spots and camps throughout each day. The Torres Del Paine park itself cannot be described in words. You need to see it for yourself. Be prepared to experience all types of weather. We had sun, rain, snow, sleet all in one day which all adds to the experience (make sure you bring waterproofs). The refugios are warm and comfortable, and have good food and drink. Note that we camped at Francis and it was too cold (Early October) so we paid extra to check in to a room at Paine Grande. We are fairly competent hikers (we completed the Salkantay trek the week before this), and I have to say that it is not a walk in the park. The hikes are challenging (particularly day 1 and 3) and you'll be sore and tired at the end of each day - Especially if the weather isn't great. The Active Trek means you do the Grey Glacier and back in one final day, but if you are worried about the distances, do the classic and give yourself some additional recovery time. You can also take a shorter route on day 3 by not going all the way up to Britanico. We also had to take sleeping bags and mats with us on the active which added a lot of extra weight so I'd highly recommending just hiring those at each camp/refugio if you can. Its best to travel as light as possible, so be tactical about what you take as it will be on your back for 4/5 days. Speaking of which, you'll need proper trekking backpack (Osprey Talon etc) with hip support and a rain cover, plus trekking poles (you can hire these from Chiletour). They will give you a guide of what else you need to bring but I would also highly recommend taking anti- inflammatory medication (for sore knees etc), moleskin tape (blisters), and high factor suncream. Finally, take a pair of swimming shorts because Ricci has a hot tub which you won't want to miss once you get back to Puerto Natales. You can of course book the trip yourself without a tour operator, however I don't think that our Patagonian experience would have been the same without Ricci and Chiletour - We were also more than happy to pay to have all the hassle taken off our hands. It really is a once in a lifetime experience, so I hope you enjoy it as much as we did! It was well worth the 2 x trips to the end of the earth.

review_text: This is a wonderful museum in the centre of Santiago, just around the back of the Plaza de Armas. I tried to go on a Saturday afternoon but it was closed, like much else in the city, but was very glad that I went back on a Wednesday morning and found it open. The exhibits - small statuary, masks, jewelery, mummies older than the Egyptians', textiles and some larger pieces - are world-class and the displays are uncluttered and perfectly lit. Each room has an interesting bit of history on the wall in Spanish, with an abridged English translation. I was blown away by the textiles room in particular - though I'd have liked a bit more information on the dyes. There are examples of various different methods and effects in weaving and tapestry, some of them truly ancient. All in all, a lovely bit of ancient culture in a surprisingly modern city. The gift shop has some great books and crafts.

review_text: Fantastic national park with glaciers, lakes, stunning peaks and well marked trails. The most popular trail and a must do if you have the time is the W trek (need 5 full days). We did a part of the W and would consider returning one day to do the full W or even the O. We chose to camp despite being complete beginners and owning no camping gear. No problem since you can either rent as we did in Puerto Natales or hire a pre-pitched tent at payed camping sites within the park. Tips: Go to base camp (Erratic Rock) for a free one hour lecture on trekking Torres Del Paine. Held daily around 3pm. Keep the weight down and your enjoyment of the trek high. Make sure your sleeping bag is more than adequate. Not ok, since it can and does get very cold at night, even in summer. Check your equipment throughly before heading into the park. You will be in wilderness! Buses run daily to the park run by five different companies from Puerto Natales. We were told not to worry about it being fully booked, even for the next morning. If you own your camping gear or made reservations with refugios then you can skip Puerto Natales.

review_text: We were slightly nervous about getting the bus after reading some of the reviews. However we were very pleased with the efficient service we received both on Punta Arenas to Peurto Natales & then on Peurto Natales to El Calafate. We made sure we got the luggage stickers added to our cases & kept them safe. All the buses had electronic frontages stating the destination, the bus terminal in Punta Arenas was for Bus Sur only so was very simple. Other bus terminals are joint & usually out of town, so be prepared to get a taxi or book a hotel close. We did book on line & paid more, but we needed a guaranteed date/time. There were only a few spare seats on each of our journeys so if you were not too bothered you could have booked & paid in Chile pesos at the office.

review_text: I did the Ruta de Los Salares tour with Andes Travel. Loved it. Pick up at hotel at 7am. We sew many salares, starting with Vega Quepiaco, then stopped for breakfast at Salar de Quisquiro, then Salar de Agua Calientes and Laguna Negra which offers perfect reflections of the surrounding scenery. We took tons of pictures at Mirador Monjes de la Pacana. We saw the Laguna Verde which is in Bolivia, just the other side of the border. We observed many volcans, one of them the Lascar was in eruption. We saw tons of Vicuñas, Flamingos, a Fox and a couple of viscacha (kind of Chilean rabbit). We drove as high as 4,826m above sea level, but we took it easy, we got good advice to breath correctly and nobody in our group experienced altitude sickness. Then from 2 to 3pm we had a complementary lunch in a Peruvian restaurant of Atacama. Our guide, Styven was courteous, friendly, knowledgeable and answered all my questions. The driver Gustavo was safe, the van in good shape and we were reminded to use our safety belts. I definitely recommend this tour.

review_text: We were fortunate to experience this glacier in 3 ways, each adding to the greater appreciation of the awesomeness. First, we hiked on the rocky beach, viewing the glacier from a distance and seeing the icebergs floating around in the lake and washed up on the shore. Third, we took the boat trip back across the lake, getting up super close to the glacier, drinking Pisco Sours with glacial ice cubes, and finally staying overnight at Lago Grey Hotel to enjoy the views of the glacier from a soft and comfy bed. Wonderful!!

review_text: Based on the other reviews I was going to skip this place, but it was Monday and this was the only museum that was open. Yes, the lighting is poor in many rooms and some of the displays could benefit from better spaces. However, the gran sala with 54 large 17th cent. paintings from Cuzco based on the life of St. Francis is really interesting. The clothing, food, instruments, etc. in the paintings all give a clue for what life was like 350 years ago. Also, there are a few gruesome and melodramatic paintings by Melchor Perez Olguin that are fun in a post-modern context. The courtyard is just lovely to relax in. The admission fee is only 1.000 so you're not out much $$ if you don't like the place.

From my husband’s trail description, I had pictured a pretty vertical hike the whole way, but it leveled out in some areas and weaved through a nice forested area up until about the 2nd camp, then it was a bit steeper with less break. Didn’t particularly notice the wind on this hike and we had a gorgeous clear day!

review_text: Our hotel, Courtyard by Marriott, recommended this company and we are delighted. We were picked up and dropped off at our hotel. review_text: If you can handle the Mt. Washington-like drive to the ski area, definitely head this way, toward sunset if you can. We were there on a cold winter day; while the rest of the party hiked around on the glacier, I sat in the cozy cafe, near a woodstove, and enjoyed tea. The food there looked really quite good, and the prices were surprisingly reasonable. You can take a ski lift higher up, but the price for that is not what I consider reasonable--but it was too cold for me to even contemplate that option anyway. The sunset was gorgeous, and then the cafe and ski area shut down, and we all drove back down the volcano in a long line.

We decided for Fjords del Sur as the sea can get very tough and we wanted a bigger boat. The boat was really nice, comfortable seats with enough space, a kiosk and restrooms. We. Ould also go outside with life jackets. The sailing was for about 1 hour and we saw some Wales and sea lions in the water. The highlight was the stop on the island. The penguins are so cut and you are allowed to walk a small track on the island. The penguins are respected and the really good guides take care of them. On the way back we saw some more whales and the captain drove slowly and switched the engine off so that we could watch the whales for some minutes. All in all a perfect tour, thanks to Guillermo our guide and the captain and the whole crew. As the sea was a bit rough it was definitely good to pay a bit more but to be on a bigger boat. Enjoy it and RESPECT THE PENGUINS! keep in mind, you are entering a strangers home. So be respectful.

review_text: I love this reservation. To get to the administration it is 2km uphill, cars cannot go up so you have to leave the vehicle downstairs. Fire is prohibited so if you go camping, you must bring a stove. We did the short trails because we went only for the day and nothing to say, they are completely worth it. The first: Aliwenmahuida, a short and easy trail, it took us less than an hour and we spent a lot of time taking photos of the landscape and lizards. The final half is being remodeled to make that trail more inclusive, which I find great! It has a beautiful viewpoint. The second: Cerro el Peine, in my opinion it is a short trail with medium difficulty, it says that the average time is 3 hours. It has a viewpoint on a giant stone with an impressive view! If you continue going up, you reach a mini waterfall that is formed from the melting ice forming a mini pool but it cools a lot after having climbed up there, it has an incredible view. The third: Los Concones, this trail is short and easy, you reach two viewpoints with views similar to the first trail. This trail is inside the campsite. We did not stay at the campsite but to give you an idea, it has bathrooms and showers with cold water, the sites have a water tap, a structure for cooking and a picnic table. They are spacious, they easily fit 2 tents. There are no businesses or anything to supply. The last trail we did was Río Lircay. In my opinion, this path is of medium difficulty, because to access the river you have to go down a rocky path, which when going down is easy but I'll take care of the return hahaha, the same thing but uphill. Perfect pools are formed to take a dip, ice-cold but delicious water for a hot day. We were very satisfied.

review_text: If you've arrived in La Serena and haven't booked a tour of Islas Damas - don't worry, we didn't either. There is a bus stop next to the Japanese gardens by the side of the motorway (headed north). If you arrive at 8.45am then the bus will arrive shortly after. It costs approx. 5000 Chilean pesos (each way) and takes the old bus approx. 2 hours (each way). Once there we joined a bunch of others on a boat (10000 Chilean pesos per person) and enjoyed a great tour of the islands, seeing: Seals, sea otters, pelicans (I think), Peruvian boobies (I'm sure), and of course the main event - I saw my first penguin! An actual penguin! That actually walked that actual penguin walk! There was on this occasion no sightings of whales nor dolphins and after the tour there is a bit of a long wait until the bus returns but I doubt you will regret the trip! Enjoy!

review_text: Valparaiso Cathedral En la Plaza Victoria al inicio de la Avenida Pedro Montt. Since 2003 it has been a National Historic Landmark. After the earthquake of 1906 the construction of the new Cathedral began in 1910 under the invocation of the Virgin of Carmen. It opened on 29 January 1950. The 1971 earthquake left it severely damaged, losing its original dome, and the 1985 earthquake caused further damage. The dome was later repaired but without following the original project faithfully. Its bell tower can be seen from several blocks around, serving as a reference point. Its plan is shaped like a Latin cross, with a central nave and two sides.

I strongly do not recommend going there in a polluted day (unfortunately, most of the days in Santiago). Probably Sundays are the best days (or after a rainy day) in order not to miss the incredible Andes range views. I rated it as 4 out of 5 because there is nothing else than a big empty space up in the top. No souvenir shop (I wanted a Costanera Center miniature for my collection), no vending machine, no multimedia room, etc; at least there are restrooms... if they improve that, I'd rather gave them 5 out of 5 stars. There is a small souvenir shop after you go out the elevator in your way down. I totally recomend getting to Sky Costanera if you are in Santiago.

review_text: There was no tour bus. It was just an older van that was difficult to get in and out of. The tour was basic sightseeing, and just included splitting one bottle of wine (no tasting) and side of the road empanadas (only one per person) even though the tour lasted hours and we were starving at that point. Review of: Punta Arenas & Strait of Magellan Park Value Excursion Dear Sean, I am sorry you felt dissapointed, and I wish you have brought this up with me directly, as I was the one conducting the tour on Christmas day, and it was our impression we did a great tour, considering the feedback we received that day. The tour included private driver, Chilean-American private guide, a firewood baked, slow cooked, grass-fed beef empanada, bottled water, a 1 lt. bottle of Chilean wine for 4, and also a traditional calafate alfajor. We, and our countless happy travelers, consider that unmatched value for this type of tour in this area. We also visited Parque del Estrecho, Nao Victoria, Plaza de Armas, Cemetary and Cerro La Cruz. We could have delved deeper, but we were requested to make the tour shorter as you guys planned to travel that evening. I would also like to know what else was expected, since the "basic sightseing" was everything that we offered in the tour itinerary, and we also added extraordinary stops such as the English cemetary and the HMS Beagle docking site. Nonetheless, we are grateful for your preference, it was our pleasure to meet you and we hope you guys enjoy the rest of your stay in this region.

review_text: The Death/Mars Valley is very close to San Pedro, about 3 km away from the center. You can walk or bike there easily. After passing through the gate and buying a ticket, it is still a kilometer or a kilometer and a half to drive/walk/bike. There you'll see the major sand dune where most people seem to stay sandboarding. The actual viewpoint is still roughly another 600 meters hike away. It is not much, but quite strenuous because of the sand and heat. The view from above is worth it - impressive Martian landscapes, with beautiful mountains in the background. It is not as large and diverse as the Moon Valley, but certainly worth a visit.

review_text: My wife and I came across Atacama Desert Stargazing during our trip, and while we're novices when it comes to astronomy, we were excited to try it out. We both watched the most recent version of 'The Cosmos' with Neil Degrasse Tyson, and this served as a great refresher to a lot of what we had learned. Afterwards, we spent time looking at the stars and the moon through a number of different telescopes. I've never really had the opportunity to look through so many high-powered telescopes, and this was awesome! Jorge also took pictures with our camera through the telescopes - so now we'll have these memories forever! We would definitely recommend this to anyone interested in astronomy and stargazing.

review_text: If you’re thinking about booking this tour - DO IT RIGHT NOW. Since were running a bit late due to the fact that Gabriel saved us last minute, we got on the road and first stopped at a coffee shop - here we got to taste a local liqueur made of grapes and try traditional Chilean pastries. It was great to have a few snacks before hitting the wine trail! Next, we headed to the first of three wineries, Casas del Bosque, where we got to taste 4 wines in a beautiful tasting room. The Riesling was divine! My favorite winery, Bodegas RE, was next on our tour. We were first led into the cellar, where they showed us traditional fermentation techniques in clay pots. Next, we were able to sit outside in the sun and enjoy our tasting as well as a tasting of their olive oils and vinegars that they make in house. They also took us into their fermentation room for liqueurs as well. Make sure you try the orange wine (omg!) and the Chardo-noirs (both white and red). Following our time at Bodegas RE, we headed to Tanino for an amazing lunch at Casas del Bosque. And lastly, we closed out our tour at Veramonte with a tasting of four wines. This winery was huge and in such a beautiful setting. The scale of production was also incredible to see. Gabriel is an amazing guide - he is so incredibly knowledgeable about everything Chile as well as the local wines. I learned so much on this trip! review_text: Mauricio has become like an extension of our family in Chile. We completed our third tour with him on November 19th. He adjusts the itinerary as we go to ensure we get an opportunity to enjoy the food, wine and cultural experiences that match our interests and tastes. On our first trip in 2007 I was looking for Malbecs but my wife and I feel in love with Carmenere. Mauricio adjusted the itinerary to ensure we got to sample some of the best Carmeneres. He also introduced us to razor clams and taught us about biodynamic and organic processes in wine production that made better wines and also addressed my sulfite sensitivities. We also were introduced to the Montes Purple Angel and the Story behind the Angel on the Montes label. We returned in 2010 to a longer stay and overnights at some of the wineries. La Casona at Matitec has become a favorite. On the last day of this trip Mauricio surprised us with a Purple Angel from 2007, which was the year of our first trip, and we drank it overlooking the yacht harbor at Vina del Mar. We also bought several cases of wine at both wineries and a wine store. We were able to bring it all back home, bubble wrapped and shrink wrapped. Duties upon re entry were minimal as the wine we brought back was not for resale but personal consumption. On our third trip we revisited La Casona, toured 11 boutique wineries and brought home phenomenal wines we can't find in the US in most cases because they are low volume production and in some instances Icon wines not sold outside Chile. This time we had a gourmet meal Mauricio worked out with the chef at House with perfect wine pairings. Mauricio has completed Sommelier, viticulture and wine making programs which has given him tremendous knowledge of all aspects of wine making, food pairing and how to adjust wine buying to your individual tastes. I give Chilean Wine Lovers my highest recommendation. No other tour has provided the range of experiences, the quality of food and wine pairing, and the level of individual attention we have had. The fact that Mauricio knows key people at nearly every winery, the major restaurants and has connections at excellent hotels makes it possible to ensure you will have an incredible experience tailored to your interests, tastes and budgets.

review_text: We walked from our hotel Crown Plaza to the La Vega Central market around 10am in January, before it got too hot. On the way there, we walked through the area where there were a number of ethnic markets/restaurants - Chinese, Korean, etc. The traffic around La Vega Central was quite congested. It was a large place. There were a lot of stores/stands inside the covered structure of the open market, and there were many stands outside as well. Many locals shop here, pulling their little carts. There were many many fresh vegetables and fruits. I was amazed at the very big and fat corn on the cobs - not sure what kind they were. And the huge watermelons looked so nice! I wish we could have gotten one, if we were not staying in a hotel .... What we were very amazed was the fact that, in such hot weather, and with so much food, there was not a single fly! Don't quite know what they did to accomplish this! Come to think of it, the central mercado where mostly seafood was sold, did not have flies either! Amazing! This La Vega Central market was much bigger than the market in Barcelona and was more local. It was rather crowded, but mostly with locals shopping there. We enjoyed the visit!

review_text: My wife and I took the Metro several times during our stay in Santiago from December 22, 2016 through January 12, 2017. The Metro is very busy even though the long trains run about every 3 minutes during the day. They are often packed with people because about 1 million people take the Metro every day. The Metro is the easiest and quickest way to get around the city. It was very clean and free of graffiti. I didn't see any paper tossed on any floor in the stations, the steps or the boarding platforms. Most of the trains are clean and modern although some are a bit older. Using the Metro was easy. When you go down into the station, there is a ticket room with cashiers. You can purchase a card and you can place any amount of pesos on the card you wish. When you go through the turnstiles, you simply waive the card in front of the yellow light and it deducts the fare from the card. Alternatively, you can purchase a one time ticket (2 tickets cost us 1,320 pesos) and you simply insert the ticket into the slot on the turnstile. To determine the direction you want to go, you simple need to know the last stop on that Metro line and go to the side of the platform that heads in that direction. You can also transfer from one line to another line by simply following the directions as you exit the train. There is no additional cost if you transfer from one line to another. If it is the stop you want, you simply go to the "SALIDA" (exit) and that will take you to the street level and out of the Metro. I think the Metro is safe although I was warned about pickpockets and I took necessary precautions. I never had a problem. I was also impressed with the courtesy, kindness and generosity of the Chileans which I repeated observed. Chileans would often get up and offer their seat on the train to an elderly woman. They were also kind to us in volunteering to help us find our way even though they did not speak English and we did not speak Spanish. I was very impressed with the genuine goodness of the Chileans. The Metro is fun, efficient, clean, safe, economical and a must for any visitor to Santiago. It is easy to do and you should not be deterred or afraid of getting lost or of being unable to figure out the Metro system.

review_text: In order to come to this place you need to be in a certain state of mind - this place is far from what the typical fat American expects of a top notch foreign ski destination. As someone who is trying to break the mold, this place is amazing - only 15 named runs, yet there are as many slopes to ski as your imagination will allow you to traverse. The "slingshot" lifts will take you to terrain so far from outside of what you'd expect in north America that you almost don't know what to do once your up there. Past reviews have trashed the place for having limited terrain and nothing challenging. The bottom line is that this is not the place for beginners, and is a complete paradise for advanced and expert skiers. The resort presents you with a beautiful canvas of 14,000 foot peaks and gives you very few boundaries to have to contemplate. If you're a decent skier looking for a good place to take on above average terrain, wait for spring in Summit County in Colorado. If you know that you're in great shape and can handle altitude of the resort, the mixed snow conditions, and be not afraid of skiing some of the continuously steepest terrain in the world, then Portillo is the place for you. Anyone who gave a bogus review of the resort wasn't good enough to ski at Portillo in the first place. This place is for people that want to ski extreme terrain and have the skill to do so. If you fit this profile, you will meet amazing other skiers from around the world that are looking for the same gem that you are, and due to the fact that this place is so remote, you won't run into anyone else. If you know that you're a 10, and are looking for a 10 experience, then go to this place. If you question what kind of skis you need to ski here, or think that you might get bored, stick with the American staples. This place gives the best skiers out there something to strive for; everyone else should settle for a lesser experience in one fo the intermediate havens that the Western U.S. has to offer.

review_text: My friends and I passed through Punta Arenas on our way to/from Torres Del Paine. We loved this cemetery so much, we spent 2+ hours in it on both trips through the city. It's vast, varied, with structures and sites in various stages of decay. The class stratification is on full display as you walk along massive concrete stacks with small square altars that give way to ornate family tombs that look more european. The cypress trees lend a surreal feeling, beautifully sculpted. We wandered and took pictures for hours, enjoying the quiet, and marveling at the diversity of family names and backgrounds. A very special place.

review_text: Santiago's better known landmark is a huge hill at the northeastern corner of the city center, with a large steel statue of the Virgin Mary at the top, serving as a viewpoint. review_text: My plan is to never go back to this theater. We went to see The Nutcracker in December, which is summer time in Santiago, Chile: 1. We got there a max of 5 min late and were not allowed to get in until the intermission 55 min later. It is a rule in this theater and after the intermission I was able to understand the reasoning behind this rule. 2. It is an old theater and I am sure it was beautiful long time ago. Today, you can see, feel, and smell the decadence because lack of maintenance. It had very little space to get in/out our seats (Anfiteatro 4th floor, 21 and 31) with super narrow and dark halls and aisles. I could understand then how such small space with no light did not facilitate anyone on a late arrival. Still, people were still allowed to get up from their tiny seats at any time during the performance, make everyone stand for them to get out, and walk the dark halls to go to the bathroom. I did not appreciate the double standard. 3.The seats were VERY tiny (and we are skinny and small humans!). The seat size is about the seating in kindergarten classrooms or a toddler chair. #21 was in a corner behind a column were I could not fit one of my legs and could barely see the performance. #31 was occupied by someone that decided just to seat there and the usher told my husband to seat on the dirty and smelly steps/floor that people use to get in/out. 4. Expensive for the quality of seats: $21,000CLP/$35USD/each 5. No air conditioner, fans, windows or any kind of ventilation. It was very, very hot and made the whole experience very uncomfortable. In my opinion, this was the worst part.

review_text: A sure way to escape the smog and if there the rain of Santiago, is to go for a hike in the Valle Nevado area. Leaving Santiago you slowly climb up the mountains through a well paved road and in a lovely environment. The cyclist slowly pedalling their way up, give you an impression how steep the sloops actually are. Just before the road to Farellones start, a weak sun breaks through the clouds, finally changing to full and bright sunshine along the road up to the mountains. For bikers is must be an incredible challenge. But those speeding down the hill, tell you that their goals were achieved that day. The road remains curvy with great views en looking at the valley you see the effort it must have cost to build it. When up the hill after 40 hairpin bends, entering Farellones area, we decided to continue our journey to Valle Nevado, approximately another 10 kilometres. This road brings you through a wealth of rocky formations with a large variety of colours, where at the background the smoggy clouds of Santiago form a picturesque entourage. Stopping at various places is a must just to enjoy the spectacular views and various wild life which is present. Entering the village Valle Nevado you can park your car at the lift area and buy a ticket for the lift at the shop. It is expensive and do not expect to get up to the top, as it only goes halfway. This is just silly and the owners should really extend this with the next lift (and for the same price!). From the top of the lift we decided to walk around and finally back down to the lift area, while visiting the desolated village itself. The village might be a good starting point for hiking as well, especially if you do not want to pay for the lift, and use your car to get up to the village. Views are great, hiking is moderately difficult and paths are clearly visible in the dry season. But above all the clear skies and warm weather made our trip worthwhile, compared to the rainy city. A day well spent!

Neruda, a lover of the sea and all things maritime, built the home to resemble a ship with low ceilings, creaking wood floors, and narrow passageways. review_text: Our family travelled 1.5hrs from Pucon to Heurquehue. GPS error added an extra 15 min. Road in is mostly gravel, with steep gradients, sharp bends and great views. We had a Subaru Forrester but most cars were 2WD. CONAF entry charge is approximately P10,000 per adult, children U12 free, with no credit cards accepted. Having an AWD meant we could drive a further 2km up a challenging road/track to a river ford that gave access to the camping ground and Refugio Tinquilco Car park on private property was P2000 for the day. The walk with our 7,9,16yo sons was spectacular. Views of Vulcan Villarica and Lago Caburga. Track undulates for 750m throuh heavily wooded forest after entering park before the climb commences. Generally track is good, with wooden steps/ramps in difficult bits. Wet and muddy sections in approx fifteen spots, along with some rocky scrambles require good hiking boots rather than runners or thongs. Our youngest son's runners were soaked and muddy within an hour. We were surprised to see families with toddlers and babies given the grade of climb. Hike to first minor lake (Lago Verde) took 2hrs, with a further 45min to Lago Chico and Lago Toro. Monkey puzzle trees and many birds added to the spectactular lake views. We took 20min of the upward hike to visit the first waterfall. We sighted many small lizards and had the good fortune to see a tarantula out of its normal season. This six hour hike was certainly worth the drive. Rangers are helpful and walk the route. Water is plentiful but some flows are sullied from the tracks above.

review_text: When you arrive to this park, you may not bring in any backpacks. You will leave them with the old man who takes your payment of 2.000 pesos to enter the park. It only takes between one and two hours to make your way through the trails so you won't need much with you on your walk. The park is VERY well maintained and clean. It is pretty small and was very quiet and empty when I went in February! There are beautiful paths that are all a bit different from each other but each magical in their own way as they lead you to some spectacular lookouts over the ocean. Walking through some parts of this park made me feel like I was walking through a story book that took place in a fantasy garden. It was one of my favorite things about Valdivia. Afterwards, you can also walk down to the beach to relax. Easy to spend at least a half day in the area! When I went there was also a festia costumbrista down the road which I visited after for some fresh local food and drinks. Definitely check it out!

review_text: This was the first stop for our bus tour of the park. We were off the bus and down to the edge as quickly as two feet could walk and it was breathtaking. The cascades were lively, there was mist rising from portions and we were occasionally sprayed with the light mist giving us a pleasant, cooling sensation. There were no other visitors at the time so our group of 40 had the area to ourselves and we managed to find several vantage points from which to capture the moment. The entire park is full of these moments and would be well worth a longer visit, starting with these cascades. This is not wheelchair accessible and for those using canes or walkers, I don't recommend trying the trail as it is short but steep with no hand holds. This is truly outdoors and not for anyone who is physically challenged unless they are willing to settle for the view from the road, which isn't bad.
