review_text: We arranged a full day tour to Torres del Paine for three people, well in advance of our trip. We paid, received email confirmations, and two days before the tour we also received a reminder with the pickup time and date. On the day of the tour we waited and waited - and no-one arrived to pick us up. Our hotel staff helped us to make multiple phone calls to the two numbers listed on the invoice. Nobody answered. With great effort and help from our hotel and neighbors we scrambled to find another tour for the same day - by luck there was a different company with a tour leaving two hours later with three spaces left in the van. The new tour was significantly cheaper than the price offered by Todo Patagonia. It was a near miss. We only had one day in Puerto Natales and one chance to see Torres del Paine before moving on to Argentina. Todo Patagonia almost ruined this part of our trip with their negligence. Later that morning we finally did get a response from the company saying that they had forgotten to put us on the list for the tour. Sure, they apologized for making a mistake and issued a prompt refund, but sadly, it was way too little, much too late, and it doesn't make up for their irresponsible and incompetent behavior. If, like us, you are planning to visit Puerto Natales at great effort and expense, choose a more reliable company. You might be the next "unfortunate mistake" they make. We regret what happened, due to your bad experience with us, we changed our reservation protocols, and verification of reservations, so that none of our passengers have a bad experience like the one you had, as we indicated at the time, we apologize and We reimbursed the money paid by you, we also offered compensation at a local restaurant, which unfortunately did not take.

review_text: We had a really bad rainy day when we took the tour, but it wasn't going to spoil the day. The tour got delayed a bit because the boat's tender process was really slow, but the tour waited for everyone. We had a nice bus that though wasn't very comfortable, it suited the tour perfectly. We started off with a short drive around puerto Chacabuco and the next town over Puerto Aysen. The towns aren't that developed but they were in one of the most gorgeous parts of Chile, so there was no shortage of breathtaking vistas. They took us around the roads in the area, where our guide explained things about the history and culture of the Aysen region. It was very informative. At some point we went to an old hanging bridge to take photos, then to a regional visitors center for a stop. The place had bathrooms, but little else. It was relatively new and with the downpour we had outside, we couldn't walk around the grounds. On clear days there are hiking trains you can take in the area. After that they took us to an agritourism farm where we had a nice lamb made in the traditional Patagonian way and had a show of typical regional dances. Very nice in total. They treated us well and let us run around the farm and take pictures of the animals (they even had 3 alpacas in the back). All in all, the tour was very satisfying and we got to learn a lot about the region. Money well spent.

review_text: Went in early April at the end of a hot day (6 pm). We wished we'd gotten there earlier! I think we could have stayed bobbing in the Cejar for hours--it was super fun to float and do crazy tricks in the water. It was such a unique experience--where else can you do this, other than in the Dead Sea? The water was a little bit chilly--but once you get in it was fine, especially on a hot day. It is also extremely clear--you can see your toes if you extend them beneath you, and "stand" in the water. What you can't see is the bottom of the laguna--so it must be very very deep! But no matter--you float easily. We self drove; it's only a half hour from San Pedro. 15K CHP (about $22 USD). Cold showers, nice clean bathrooms, and changing rooms available (tip: shower on the sunny side of the showers for extra warmth!). DO NOT dunk your head/ears/hair in the water. The ends of my friend's hair got wet and it turned into a brittle, salty mess, and she was cleaning salt out of her ear for days after accidentally dunking one.

review_text: Thomas Poussard was our local guide after the 14-day Golden Princess cruise in South America on Feb 15, 2014. When we interacted with him on-line before the booking, he was very responsive within 24 hours all the time and clear in communication on our expectation and the arrangement. When he picked us up at the Valparaise terminal, we realized that he just came back from a trip to his hometown in France due to a family need. He made sure that he came back in time for our appointment instead of handing off to somebody else. When he realized that we had quite a load of luggage, he hired a driver for our two day tour so that he could spend full time with us while the driver not only just drove us around but also watched our luggage. So we wasted no time in parking or anything but just hit the right places, without worrying about the valuables. Thomas knew the area well -- knowing when to be at where. Knowing that I am interesting in good scenery photography, he took us to the hill for the panoramic view early in the morning at Valparaise before the cloud and mist came in from the sea later in the morning. For photography, that is the day and night difference. With the journalist major, Thomas was knowledgeable in history of Valparaiso, Santiago, and Chile, and gave us plenty of short stories. The restaurants he took us were excellent in choice, taste, and price. Thomas attended to details. Mike and Adolfo took safety precautions every step of the way and not once did I question their gear, their competence, their professionalism, nor their genuine love of climbing! They were also very encouraging, so it felt like climbing with my own friends back home in the states. Their English is great, too, so there was no language barrier. We climbed for hours, and took a break for a great picnic lunch with mate. I really didn't want the day to end. If I had more time I would've climbed even more days. Whenever anyone asks me about my trip, I ALWAYS start with the day I went climbing, and then I talk about all the other incredible things I did in Chile!

review_text: Felipe Sunkel (aka Chaura) was the first guide we met on arriving in Torres del Paine. He is a huge guy, nice to look at and is immediately warm and engaging. “Bigger than life” comes to mind. Chaura is knowledgeable about the locale and no question was dumb or inconsequential. A geologist by training he is well-versed in landscape formation, as well as micro-weather patterns, flora, fauna, local history, food and drink. Chaura has been guiding since he could hold down a job and relays information with pride in his surroundings. His certification as a Wilderness First Responder added to the safety I felt while with him. Chaura's respect and admiration for all things Earth is evident in the way he lives. During days off from guiding in Chile he spent a week building a trail in French Valley. On a tour of U.S. national parks with us he picked up bits of trash and, at trails’ end he’d properly dispose of cig butts, paper, plastic stickers, hang tags and candy wrappers from his pocket. I have also seen him with animals where he projects trustworthiness to acquire seemingly inhuman proximity. At a state park he came within feet of desert big horn sheep. Later he got our notoriously shy senior cat to eat from his hand, a first for a stranger with her. Children take to Chaura right away, and he is skilled at imparting knowledge without child-speak. Chaura’s constant good-nature, sense of humor and spiritedness are a pleasure to be with for extended periods. review_text: We booked 4 tours and a transfer with Turistour and regretted it. 3/5 of our pickups were later than the half an hour window suggested, leaving us wondering if we had been forgotten (including our transfer to the airport). For the geysers tour we had to be ready for 04:30 and weren't picked up until 5:20 (all the more frustrating when you have woken up at 3-something). after the 1.5 hour journey, the guide then told us we had "a few minutes" at the geysers before we had to eat a distinctly average breakfast and move on. not really worth the CH10,000 (~US$15) entry in addition to the cost of the tour. we then had half an hour at the hot springs, which are only hot in one very small section (there are A LOT of people there as all tours go at the same time). we then went to a 'village' that isn't actually a village - its a row of shops selling the usual tourist souvenirs (noone lives there). We had plenty of time there though so i guess it was worth cutting our time short at the geysers... It is worth stressing how cold it is at the geysers (the agency didn't do so) - i wore a base layer, fleece and thick down jacket and it was just about enough. i only had one layer on my legs and that was cold. take gloves and wear hiking boots if you have them. On the Moon Valley tour we also seemed to whistle past the actual 'Moon Valley' part in order to rush round a number of other less interesting sites. the views there are really out of this world and most groups seemed to be walking along the ridge taking it in, hearing about it from the guide along the way. we got to the lookout point and were given 10 minutes free time. so we walked the ridge ourselves for 4 minutes, took a picture and turned back to find our guide in a hurry to get back to the bus. Death/Mars Valley was the same if not worse. we drove as far as we needed to pay the entry fee, stopped in a shaded part of the valley so we could take a (rubbish) picture, got back on the bus and drove back out. The comfort of your journey is also a bit of a lottery - one we lost more times than we won. on one trip i had to sit in the last of 4 seats on the back row of a minibus. there was approximately 4 inches of shoulder space remaining between the 3 men already on the row so i had to lean forward perched on the end of the seat for the 4 hours we spent on the bus. we asked in the agency if they could ensure it doesn't happen again. they said there was nothing they could do and sure enough the next day, i was on the back row (although this time only 3 of us) and my girlfriend on the seat where leg room is entirely replaced by a wheel. half way through the journey we then picked up a random guy that needed a ride back to san pedro... he was ushered to the last remaining seat on the back row by the guide until i told him it wasn't happening. The guides' English varied considerably between our tours. the basics were always there but we had the full spectrum - from really excellent detail and descriptions of what places were, how they were formed etc. (on our tour of the lagunas altiplanicos with Diego) to simply, when to get on and off the bus and what the places were called. I would strongly recommend against using this agency (although i cannot vouch for any of the others). on reflection, we wished we had just hired a car and/or bicycle and done it ourselves, in our own time and without sharing it with the 30 or so other tour buses being herded around like a school trip in a hurry. Maybe Turistour will reply to this review, maybe not. But we did raise our issues both to our guides and in the office and they were unwilling to do anything at the time. So despite what the feedback forms they hand out at the end of every tour would suggest, it seems they're not actually willing correct or improve their service.

I suggest to have enough time for this place and go up there with a cable car and walk down on foot.

review_text: Neruda's poetry has lighted my way though life since I was 15 or so. I was keen to explore his homes in Chile during my visit in 2013. I loved La Sebastiana in Valparaiso. But my Chilean friends and I were turned away at Isla Negra because they were booked out (mainly by school groups, who were occupied splashing each other in the green waters of the Oceano Pacifico, alas!). So, I was determined to step into La Chascona when I arrived in Santiago by bus. Fairytale-like, every nook and corner celebrates Neruda's secret love for singer Matilde Urrutia, whose untamed red curls gave the house its name (in the Quecha language). The superb audio-guide in English that came with my ticket allowed me to look for unforgettable details: a double-faced painted portrait of Urrutia the singer, for instance, has a tiny face of Neruda buried in her neck. Rich with crockery, furniture and artefacts of their life together, La Chascona today celebrates their love, his poetry ~ and her spirited restoration of the house, damaged in a military coup, after Neruda's death in 1973. La Chascona was by far my favourite attraction in Santiago.

review_text: Santiago Metropolitan Cathedral is located in the city's historic center and faces the northwest corner of Santiago's Plaza de Armas. It is the seat of the Archbishop of Santiago de Chile and the center of the archdiocese of Santiago de Chile. Construction of the neoclassical cathedral began in 1753 and ended in 1799. The architect was the Italian Gioacchino Toesca. Further alterations ordered at the end of the 19th century gave it its present appearance. Previous cathedrals in the archdiocese had been destroyed by earthquakes. Certainly would very highly recommend visiting this cathedral to any tourist in Santiago to appreciate the fine architecture.

review_text: If you want to see all the atractions, you must to go to San Cristobal. When you arrive to the gates of San Cristobal you could choose bay foot or by funicular. In both you can stop on Zoo or see differents botanicals gardens and other place to take rest and make a barbacue or picnic. 2) Take subway and descend on Pedro de Valdivia, you will see a very beautiful and chic place on Santiago "Providencia" in this area yo can eat, drink and walk very quiet (not in Baquedano), you will walk trought Pedro de Valdivia Norte, crossing Río Mapocho, the view is more beautiful than Baquedano. When you arrive at gates of San Cristobal you only can up by foot, because the cable way is on maitenance. You can ascend by in middle of forest trails. On both ways you ascen to the climber, the most beautiful way to see Santiago and buy souvenirs or drink traditional MOTE, you will never forget this amazing beverage. I Hope you came!!! And if you are a biking person, you will be so much happy!

review_text: Easy to get to by colectivo taxi, about 25 minutes. Beautifully curated. It followed the peoples of this coastal area for thousands of years. The "mummies" are the draw, but the exhibits, history, and anthropology are the reward. There are far more mummies in the Arica museum on Colon 10, but not so easy to see and photograph there. This museum also had embryo and premature baby mummies. The explanations are in Spanish, but there are computers in each hall of the museum at the entrance with English translations. . The mummies are in the second hall which is on your left, but no English assistance there. Buy your admission at the reception on your right to get into both. Lovely grounds. Allow extra time for your return. You will need to walk to the main highway and to your left a ways to the collectivo stop or you can flag down these yellow taxis. Usually they are abundant, but the day of our visit there was a religious festival up the road and all the taxis that passed were full. After 45 minutes we called our hotel to send a taxi, and then one not coming from the festival stopped and picked us up. Worth the excursion if you enjoy history and anthropology.

review_text: Reading through some of the reviews - the negative ones seem to be where people have tried to do it independently (which is how we normally travel but…). We’re all tourists so be one and travel with a small group and a knowledgeable guide to maximise your time. We travelled with Alabalti Atacama who were excellent. There were 15 of us in a white minibus - picked up on time and well informed about how the day would operate and more importantly - where the ‘banos’ stops would be! Started at 3:30pm - just a 10min drive from amazing San Pedro to the park entrance. Everything was sorted in advance so just a quick banos stop! And then we drove to the far end of the park and oh my, at every turn in the road, there was another awesome view that was difficult to capture with a mere phone camera. We had 5 stops in total (which I’m pretty sure would be standard with any excursion): 1. End of the park, Three Marys (no walking) 2. Rock formation stop - 5mins walking 3. Amphitheatre - 10mins walk downhill 4. Great Dune - walk 15-20mins each way in sand, but we had 3 stops going up and boy is the view worth it from the top. 5. Snack stop with drinks & nibbles 6. Sunset stop around 8pm - no walking. So wear hiking boots or similar as otherwise you’ll constantly have dirt and sand to shake out! Obviously apply sunscreen and one of those fab hats you can buy in town with the string as it will be windy. T-shirt and shorts fine but you will need a layer and waterproof for the sunset stop - but you can leave all this on the bus at the other stops! The bus carries drinking water so you can be topped up whenever. So bite the bullet and take a tour - so much easier…

review_text: After meeting Juan Paolo (J) in Plaza de Armas, we took the subway to Departmental in the San Miguel area and walked a few blocks to the area of the Open Sky Museum. On a warm afternoon, I was the only participant and, in addition to sharing his knowledge of the art and history, Juan Paolo was considerate, finding shady spots and seats, where possible, so that I could rest. The area is flat but open and the heat beats down on concrete so drink lots of water. Over 50 pieces of art, chosen by each block's residents from those submitted by the artists, grace the end walls of the flats. We discussed the artists, subjects and related history. My one disappointment was not sharing a meal with locals, as advertised. If there is a minimum number of participants required, the itinerary should be updated to reflect this. We returned to La Starria by subway and went to a cafe but the "meal" was minimal, a medialuna and limonade for me, salad for J. Juan Paolo's knowledge as a history teacher is considerable and he willingly shared this and chatted about many topics. Thank you for a great afternoon, J. Review of: Small-Group Tour: Open Sky Street Art Museum Including a Chilean Traditional Meal in Santiago

Chaxa is a great place to take pictures, in the middle of a salt flat where we saw more flamingoes than expected and quite near the path. Definitely worth a visit!

My first experience with Bicicleta Verde was the afternoon Parks & Politics Tour, which obviously impressed me enough to bring me back for each of the other two tours, the nighttime Ups and Downs Dawn tour and the morning Locals’ Life Tour. Each tour was different from the previous, and each as enjoyable and informative. For the first tour, a friend and I wound our way with the guide from the historic and beautiful Bellas Artes area up through residential Providencia, and back to the center of Santiago. The tour focused on the political history of Chile, and how life in the city today is compared to before and during the military dictatorship. The tour was fascinating and fun, and learning about the complicated history of Chilean politics is an opportunity that no visitor should pass up. After the tour, my friend and I met up with some of the Verde people to watch the Chile-Brasil futbol game in Bellavista. About a month later my gringa Aunt and gringo brother visited the country, so I took them on the night tour the day they arrived. It was the perfect introduction to Santiago for them, and the perfect way to relax and enjoy their first night in Chile. We started out in Las Condes, and made our way to the center Bellavista area, ending in a chic bar in Bellas Artes nibbling on delicious appetizers and sipping on their first pisco sours. The tour had focused on parks and architecture in Santiago, especially in the wealthy outer layer of Las Condes. This past week I completed my third and final (or is it??) tour with La Bicicleta Verde, the Local Life morning tour. The group- my father, the guide, and me- started in Bellavista and wound our way to the Patronato area next to the river for a tour of La Vega (the coolest outdoor fruit and veggie market) and finished up at Plaza de Armas. Not surprisingly, this tour was also incredibly informative and fun at the same time. Our experience on this tour highlights one of my favorite things about the company: the personalized service. My father, a business professor but closet history buff, mentioned to our guide at the beginning of the tour that he was interested in hearing a little about the history of Santiago and Chile. Despite its being a culture tour, Rodolfo the guide made it a point to include historical facts and stories about the city whenever possible. My dad loved the tour, and I learned a lot about Santiago that I had previously not known. Overall, I highly recommend this company to any visitors (or residents) of Chile. The tours combine the perfect amount of bike-riding, talking, and eating and drinking (snacks and drinks included in each tour). The actual act of riding the bike is not a strenuous endeavor; rather, it is easy, relaxing, and the best way to see a city- in the open air! In my opinion, La Bicicleta Verde is a model company, born very recently, but well-run and already a thriving tourist industry. The workers at Verde are young and innovative, and the tours obviously reflect this young vigor. Don’t pass through Santiago without experiencing one of these phenomenal tours. Viva la Verde!

review_text: During my three-day-stay in Quebrada de Alvarado I hiked one day to cerro el roble and the next day to Piedra del Indio located in the valley of las palmas. Cerro el Roble being the highest point of Parque Nacional La Campana offered excellent views of both los Andes including Aconcagua and cordillera de la costa. The hike in itself goes along a car trail leading up to an old russian observatorium closed down in 1973. Apart from a final tough zig-zag it was a rather easy trekking of 5 hours up and down. Piedra del Indio was my favourite between the two hikes. You see the impressive wall of stone, which is supposed to resemble the face of an indian, once you enter the valley by car through the road called las palmas. To reach the trail you need to turn left when there is a rural bus stop. The trail starts as a rather broad road and narrows in once the hike gets steeper as you walk in the shadow of forest. At the stone you can see the valley and el Roble but the real attraction for me was hiking/climbing up the right side of the rock to the two upper terraces of the rock. There are some ropes to hang on to but it's pretty secure and the level of difficulty is low although you should probably not suffer from vertigo. A real gem in my opinion.

No introduction from the guide (Carolina) other than “be prepared with the money for the tickets” you should know Tatio is a 4.500 mts of altittude and there are lots of precautions you’ll have to have for safety. After we arrived we realized Carolina had no knowledge on the Geysers formation, I saw a 5 minute video on you tube before going and was more expert than her. Worst part came when my son started feeling bad due the alttitude, she didn’t care, after three times i asked her for help she only said “he’ll be ok” whe other tours saw his condition the approached and provided assistance, then asked her for an oximeter or oxigen to help my son and she didn’t had any. We decided to wait on the trashed van making breath exercises with my son until Carolina ended her circuit without a single urge. The icing on the cake was when we where going back, the van stopped at some point and they started to fix something under it, I noticed they where fixing some parts with ropes!, and again other tours stopped by offering assistance as they noticed this wasn’t a safe condition for a mountain path with passengers. This was an unsafe, irresposible, awfull tour, and a very expensive one, never again with this agency Only good thing I can say is Felix, the driver was a lot more concerned anout my son’s condition and the rest of the group than Carolina, also he was a very good driver

review_text: We chose to do the Stargazing tour through our accommodation, where they booked a tour through Astrotour. We were surprised by how expensive the tour was (20,000$ CLP, or £25) however chose to do it anyway after hearing great feedback from previous travellers along our trip. We also later found out (after booking the tour) that it was a full moon night, and this would have a large impact on how you could see the stars. We spoke to an Astrotour representative about this, yet they said that the full moon does not impact on your ability to see the stars... this was not the case. The tour started well, picking us up from outer Hostel on time and then driving for 15 mins or so into the desert out to an outdoor observatory, with a huge telescope in the middle. Our guide Nathan didn't speak English brilliantly, and this meant that it was confusing and hard to understand his explanation on how a star is formed and it's life cycle. I know the basics regarding a stars life, so knew roughly what he was talking about- however Nathan used analogies like a car's engine and a baby to explain about a star-this would've been easier just to explain without the analogies. This went on for about 40 minutes- with no sign of us being able to use the telescope. Eventually we were allowed to use the telescope (after Nathan fiddled with it to get it working- it was not properly prepared or set up) yet we only had around 20 seconds each of time looking at the telescope- Nathan followed this up with multiple explanations of constellations and planets- showing us them through the telescope each time. Also, the full moon made a HUGE difference in our ability to see the stars and planets, with the addition of cloud. Furthermore, Nathan fiddled with the settings on our camera to take some photos of the stars and planets through the telescope. They were good photos, however he did not inform us on what he had fiddled with- this subsequently ruined our photos for the next day until we realised what the problem was. The only consolation was hot chocolate, tea and biscuits at the end- which were out of a packet anyway. Overall we had 2 minutes of time looking through the telescope... quite awful for a tour only 2 hours long and costing double the price of our valley of the moon tour, per person. The guide was not very informative and they weren't good with customer service. DO NOT do with Astrotour!!!

review_text: Rebuilt after a recent earthquake, this museum is still adding to its collection. But what we see is impressive. Being in Chile, I was interested mainly in Chilean art and artifacts, but most of the works from the Pre-Columbian period come from Peru to Mexico. My favorite room features wonderful textiles, surpassing those found in Europe, and there is plenty from the Mapuche and other local tribes. The Mapuche defeated the Incas and the Spanish and are still in a state of war mainly in the Chilean courts. They were outstanding silversmiths (still are) and traded with colonists. While not as well known to me, I was fascinated by them and the exhibits provided detailed explanations in both Spanish and English. Also take note of the very early mummies and some of the stone and wooden art of Easter Island. Sadly, other museums around the world have ripped off much Easter Island art. I might also suggest a trip to Santa Rita winery, which has an amazing private pre-Columbian, Mapuche and Easter Island collection that rivals and complements this museum, and the Underraga winery, which has many fascinating rotating exhibits that often feature indigenous people. Go on Sunday when all public museums are free.

review_text: I spent 7 days at Atacama and booked a Vacation Package with FuiGosteitrips - Zoom Atacama partner. I made the Reservation before going by indication of 3 friends who had already done the tours with them too, partial payment before arriving and the rest there the day I arrived! I was very well received and all the tours went well: Day 1 - Astronomical Tour - Guide Amadis: the quietest of all because it is a contemplative tour so it makes all the difference to have a Guide with knowledge in astronomy and Amadis was this person besides super good people! He shared with us a lot about the constellations and the stars. For those who like astrology he also goes telling where each sign is, super interesting! Important point: It is recommended to go to the new moon or as close as possible to it as this will be less bright favouring the illumination of the sky only by the stars (and ensuring those surreal photos we see there) Day 2 - Termas of Puritama and Vallecito - Driver Oscar/Guide Amadis The thermas were like a hug in the cold that I caught rs. Super worth the visit, there are 8 therms at this point (as if they were mini natural pools) being the hottest with 32o. The driver Oscar, super friendly, took us and we had around 2h to enjoy! I visited Vallecito again with the Guide Amadis. Always well-humored and giving many explanations about the history of the place, which made the whole visit much richer! He was also very patient and available to take pictures. Dia 3 - Piedras Rojas y Lagunas Altiplanicas - Guia Maurício This tour is beautiful! We arrived well and saw the sun rise, we understood about the different flamingos. Mauricio was great (speaked English and Spanish due to the demand of the group), communicated super well. All right! Dia 4 - Valle del Arco Iris y Laguna Cejar - Guias Jeferson/Camila The Valley of the Iris Arc is beautiful, one more of the landscapes to avoid. Jefferson was of light energy and up! Also was pointing us along the way some additional information, showing animals and also suggested to our group a fun photo. Laguna Cedar with Camila was great too! The first woman Guide with whom I made a tour there, was patient with photos, also gave us context about the places we passed in detail and also encouraged me in the Laguna Cejar that is super frozen but was super worth it! Dia 5 - Geyser el Tatio e Valle de la Luna - Guias Andrea e Cris Andrea is one of the funniest guides I've ever met! Super up and always telling people lightly and in detail where we were going. All my admiration for those who start the 5am day in this sympathy, I use to apologize for when I caught in sleep hahahaha the tiredness won. Day 6 - Salares Route - Guide Jaime Tour that reaches a very high altitude too (as well as basically all) but without physical effort, the whole journey is by bus with stops. Jaime was another great Guide and everything went well. Cerro Toco was not possible due to weather conditions*** and I was offered the exchange for trekking to Lascar or refund. As I was afraid because of the difficulty of the journey, I chose the refund and had no problems! Although guides are very accustomed to Brazilian tourists and always roll a portunhol, it is recommended that you have a basic notion of Spanish for better understanding of all the explanations. The landscapes are amazing but understanding the context makes everything even better! The meals included (breakfast or lunch or afternoon coffee - depending on the tour will vary) were also good - Simple but super cool and well made. Transportation was always quiet, new vehicles, gentle drivers and super punctual. All the tours were very organized with WhatsApp group before every tour. In the voucher sent before arrival there are instructions of what clothes to take, the duration of the journey and tours itself, altitude, etc. *I leave as a suggestion to review only the instructions regarding the necessary clothes, in some that constituted the need to carry only a short wind I believe that could be added to the mention of warmer jackets because the altitude varies a lot and most of the time in any shade it gets colder - in general Brazilians suffer more because we are used to milder temperatures. In short, well organized, punctual, communicative and with qualified staff! See you at the Salar de Uyuni 🙌🏼

review_text: We booked with Christian through his website and we were very glad we did as he gave us a comprehensive and thoroughly enjoyable tour of Valparaiso and Viña Del Mar. He met us at the bus station ( our bus was late) and then we went on a five hour walking tour, stopping only briefly for an empanada. We took the trolebus as well as the funiculars and shared taxi. The best parts were wandering round the alleys and paseos of Valparaiso with Christian explaining the architecture as well as the street art. It helps when someone obviously knows what he is talking about. He even showed us his childhood house and play areas. We decided we didn’t want to stop for lunch so Christian took us to an empanada shop with a wide variety of empanadas at a good price. We visited the flower clock in Viña Del Mar and got a free photo souvenir, the Castillo Wulff and walked around the area until it was time for our bus back to Santiago. Christian dropped us off at the bus station. He explained the history of the place as well as the buildings and structures we saw. He was very knowledgeable and friendly and answered all our questions. It was great to meet you and showing you our city during our full day private tour. We wish you all the best and much more travelling for this 2018!

review_text: The proximity of Valle Nevado to Santiago made it an easy escape while recently in Chile on business. As there had been no new snowfall over the period of the previous two weeks or so, I was prepared for Spring conditions. The slopes were clearly marked and well groomed. The mid-mountain restaurant and facilities were modern, and from the incredibly helpful staff at the rental center, to the ticket window, gondola, bar and restaurant, I could not have imagined a more pleasant or relaxing day. HF1clTS: What a pleasure to read such a glowing review of Valle Nevado! Our proximity to Santiago makes Valle Nevado the #1 escape from Santiago July-September, to enjoy the fresh, clean air of the Andes and ski the resort's exciting terrain. In 2016, Valle Nevado installed a new snowmaking system for those days when snowfall is light, which we hardly had to use during the season given how much it had snowed. The resort has made customer service its main focus, training our staff to understand and meet the expectations of international travelers, and we're glad to see it is paying off.

review_text: It is a perfect panorama to disconnect a little from the city and connect with nature and the culture of the people in Pomaire. BiciGreda is an excellent panorama, both for its landscapes surrounded by hills, and for the people with a tremendous closeness and willingness to show their native way of life linked to pottery. Diego, the tourist guide of the activities, puts his soul into the service he provides, his energy is tremendous and he does a remarkable job in showing and creating community in Pomaire, it is noticeable that he behaves in a very authentic way with the neighbors and with a very notable sustainable project. The plus that the project has is that by touring the streets of potters on restored bikes (very comfortable) you change the perspective and meaning of your visit, you find people living fully in their town, they integrate you into their daily life and as It says in one of its streets, they teach you the art of giving shape to the dreams that the earth dreams... together with the singing of little birds on the route, they make BiciGreda an 11/10 panorama, totally recommended!

review_text: I was looking forward to this trip so was a bit disappointed when the weather turned increasingly cloudy and wet as we approached the lake. It lived up to its name of Lago Grey! However, the glaciers in the distance could still be seen and we passed a number of icebergs that looked so small from a distance and were SO BIG close up. Our boat captain steered so close to a couple of bergs that we felt we could almost touch them. My biggest problem was keeping my camera lens dry - and one of the crew helped out by giving me some tissues from the cabin. From the photos its hard to tell it was raining. The three glaciers at the end of the lake were spectacular - each one better than the one before and all so blue. Save your photos for the last glacier. A wonderful day out arranged by the excellent Tierra Patagonia team. They arranged lunch for the two of us at a nearby restaurant after the lake cruise and nothing was too much trouble. On the way back, I couldn't get the photos of the Torres del Paine as the clouds had claimed the sky. Its a long drive back, and there is always the chance of seeing a puma (which we did).

review_text: Booked a private all day wine tour of the Casablanca Valley and it was supposed to include a lunch stop in Vina Del Mar. Everything was confirmed with Al before leaving the US, and we were excited to meet Al after reading all the reviews. Upon pick up at the cruise terminal, we discovered that Al substituted his inexperienced brother to be our wine tour guide. The scheduling wasn't right, and he had no idea we were to have lunch in VDM. He did try to accommodate us, but that only ruined the day more as we couldn't get our wine tasting at Casas del Bosque and there was no reservation for us in VDM so we just returned to the ship. We did visit Bodegas RE which was nice. Casas del Bosque looked pretty, but we really couldn't get anyone to help us there and finally managed to buy 1 bottle of wine for 6 people. The highlight of the day was Le Recova. They had a beautiful deck overlooking the vineyard with a great wine presentation and explanation with a light food pairing. Unfortunately, this was not a great experience as we did not get Al. Review of: Tasting Valparaiso: Valparaiso City & Wine Experience This day I felt a bit betrayed by these people, because we did our best for them, but they were one of those groups that were upset from the beginning. He kept blaming me for his miscoordinations; in his defense, the company he bought this tour from were not very good. I wouldn't have sold this to them, but Wineriest are a reseller and they don't do a very good job giving people information. Some facts: 1. They didn't have enough time for a full day wine tour, but booked one through Winerist anyway ()we used to operate for winerist). 2. They had added more people last minute, so the price per person would be lower. These last 2 didn't show, so they were charged for 8, and they took that frustration out on us. From the start of the day the money thing was an issue for them, so we got off on the wrong foot right away. 3. I never said I'd be their guide. 4. The Casas del Bosque visit was my treat since they were so concerned about those 2 extras that they had to pay for. I also did it so they wouldn't have to wait so long until their next winery visit. Apparently they felt it was included. It wasn't. 5. My brother is a walking encyclopedia; he's an Award Winning Tour Guide, so once again, they didn't have enough arguments for this review. They were just angry, and that's fine. This is my 50% of the story. My conclusion is that, unfortunately, many people don't buy from us directly, and buy from resellers who have not been around very long, like Winerist; and companies like this try to fit in like 12 hours worth of touring into 6 hours, and it just doesn't work. They don't know how to say to no people. So, in a way, I understand his frustration... I just think it wasn't fair to lay it all on us. If he wanted to blame us, he could only blame us for 1/6 of that day: Trying to fit all of what he wanted to do into one short shore excursion day.

review_text: One of the main reasons to visit this area is that its too close by to miss! Just 15 mins from San Pedro, you can sneak this in, in between or after the longer, more tiring day trips. Don't ignore it because you wont see this landscape elsewhere. Just follow the signs out of San Pedro, pay the entrance fee and get a map. There are 2 attractions here: the actual valley of the moon and the three marias (rock formation). We only went to the valley and unfortunately missed the three marias since we spent sunset at the valley and they did not allow us to go elsewhere after dark. Once you park for the valley of the moon, its a moderate uphill climb for about 20mins to get to the viewing areas. The views are surreal and other worldly. You may want a wind jacket and something light if you go for the sunset. There are no proper safety barriers and plenty of places to slip and fall so you need to be careful with children. This review is for the Valle de la Luna only. I believe the Valle de la Muerte/Death valley is different.

review_text: The Grand Santiago Tower is a must see when visiting Santiago! Once we arrived in Santiago, the "Costanera Centre" or "Gran Torre Santiago" is the first thing we saw. It towers over the rest of the city. Unlike some sky scarpers, it's a beautiful building and and can be seen from miles away. The tower is connected to a large shopping centre full of well known shops and restaurants. Once we were all shopped out we decided to take the long climb up the tower... Just kidding, there is a large elevator which quickly takes you to the top floor. Before entering the elevator, we paid the equivalent of £4.00 each for a ticket and were then searched for guns and sharp objects just like an airport. We didn't find this a problem, the safer the better! When we reached the top, the views were AMAZING! I've been in some high buildings with great views before but nothing like this. We picked a lovely sunny day in November 2016 and could see for miles. you get a full 360 degrees view of this beautiful city surrounded by the Andes mountains. There are telescopes fixed to the ground but really they are not needed. If you go on a clear day you can literally see for miles. This was one of the first places we visited in Santiago and I'm so glad we went. Best £4.00 I have ever spent! (note. Santiago has very bad smaug, which is a layer of smoke that sits just below the clouds. You can normally judge if it's a bad day for the smaug as it's very visible even from the ground. The locals told us to go up after it has been raining as it clears it.)

review_text: I only spent a day there to do the Mirador of Las Torres treck, but I would love to come back and see more of this Park. The landscape is truely amazing and you get to see so many different things: rivers, woods, moutains, birds, ducks, pumas is you are very lucky. It is a must in Patagonia! Try to go there for at least three days if you can. One option is to actually stay in Puerto Natales as it is cheaper but they also have small ranch houses with affordable options. This park is very rich and I will definitely come back to see more of it. If you are doing las torres track make sure you are in good health as it takes +/- 4 hours to go up and pretty much the same amount of time to go down, so block a full day for that hike. Was really worth it!

review_text: Beautiful/breathtaking scenery, but it is a shame how poorly the park is managed. The trails, mainly on the W have been highly eroded by trekkers, and there is a huge garbage and human waste problem (which has led to closing a least one campsite Campimento Italiano). The park ( again most notably the W) is in sore need of recovery. Having worked in the field of environmental management for 10 + years, it was heart breaking to see the damage park visitors cause, along with very little signage and education efforts by park management to remedy the problem. even more heartbreaking is the large expanse of fire damage (hundreds of hectares, fire started by trekkers in 2011 who lit their stove somewhere between Campimento Paso and Refugio Grey, which due to heavy winds swept quickly through he park, burning forest from that point to between Refugio Paine Grande and Campimento Italiano) which does look like it will recover any time in the near future. I hiked the full circuit trek in 8 days in a counter clockwise direction (beautiful scenery), with a guided group, Erratic Rock, which is useful if you are traveling alone and want to divide the weight of 8 days of supplies and gear and if you have not done long treks before. My pack was 20 kilos, and would have been heavier if I did this alone. I had great weather, but if the weather had been poor, certain sections, namely the John gardener pass would be dangerous to do alone. The guide was helpful, looked out for the group, and made extra efforts to make us happy, though I did not get along with him personally (to put it mildly), so I can't recommend Erratic Rock as a guide service. If you do the W you definitely do not need a guide.

review_text: Yesterday we did the free walking tour of Santiago and had a fantastic guide. Today we traveled to Valparaíso and did the equivalent tour there. Our guide today was Juanjo and he was as informative and entertaining as his colleague, Franco, was in Santiago. We gained an understanding regarding the history of Valparaíso. However, Juanjo also gave insights into the broader history of Chile. We took a 7.30am bus from Pajaritos bus station and arrived comfortably in time for a coffee before the 10am tour. We had a fantastic lunch at Fauna restaurant after the tour and eventually caught a 5.30 bus back to Santiago. The walking tour lasted 3.5 hours. The tipping suggested is 5000-10000 Chilean pesos per person. We went mid-range and thought this was great value for the money. Really worthwhile.

review_text: Got on a trip with my girlfriend and other 7 people in a van with a tour guide and a driver. We have been informed that there was no roadblocks and the road was all cleared to climb by Valle Nevado and the local police. We stayed 14 hours STUCK in the snow with RIDICULOUS support from the resort. Seeing trucks trying to get us out for a few hours and then completely leave us with no news about when we would get out, or even someone dropping by to leave a single bottle of water. Plus, had to stay other 2 days, paying dollars on the hotel (half price, but still, no clothes to change or whatsoever the expectation of spending that money on our trip) because the road was still blocked. There were riots every morning at the front desk, cases of people with broken ribs in pain and not being able to go to the hospital. To finish, we decided to go for a snowboard ride to save the experience. We dropped down a mountain but when we got at the lift, people said we couldn't go up because we didn't have the ski pass. Who in the front desk told me I needed one?! For a first-timer, this is completely new. The good part is the view which is beautiful and the manager (Alejandra) that made our experience a little bit less painful.

review_text: This tour of "Rainbow Valley", involved more than just the fascinating geology of the valley itself. It is not as well subscribed as some of the other better known destinations from San Pedro but we found it to be quite spectacular and very interesting; made more so by our very informative guide. Our first stop was at Yerbas Buenas, where we were shown a selection of the rock art there. This indicated that it was well populated in ancient times, when there was more water present. We then went to Valle Arcoiris itself and spent over an hour following a short route. We were shown the various minerals that cause such a variety of colours on the mountains, mainly greens and reds. This is a very special place and well worth a visit. One surprise is that the minerals have not been exploited; long may it continue.

review_text: We were a bit crazy - but we weren't alone. We started our hike at 2:00 am from Las Torres Hotel. We hiked much of the way in the dark with headlamps. We were fortunate that there was a full moon the night/morning that we hiked, so that helped some. The first hour or so of hiking was difficult getting up and out of the main valley and into the side valley; the second hour or so was decent; the last hour or so was tough as the climb is through a boulder/scree field from the terminal moraine of the Towers area. We were sweating and warm most of the hike, but once we made it to the top, just at sunrise!, we quickly cooled off. There were about thirty people up there with us. We got lost a couple of times, in the dark, but quickly got back on track because of the maps and GPS devices that we carried. The hike up required about four hours, and our round trip was about 8.5 hours, including about an hour at the mirador. Definitely recommended if you're in the area and capable!

review_text: Others in the forum have favorably recommended Wine Tours Valparaiso for Chilean wine tours, and I would like to emphatically agree. My wife and I had only a few days to see Santiago and Vina del Mar/Valparaiso, but we decided at the last minute that we also wanted to tour the Casablanca Valley wineries, which are between the two cities. We happened upon Wine Tours Valparaiso by a simple Google search, which also led to the recommendations on the forum. We e-mailed the address on their website the day before we wanted to go, and Michael responded within a couple of hours with options. We choose the full day wine tour, picking us up in Santiago, and dropping us off in Vina del Mar. The tour ended up being one of the highlights of our trip. Michael is a native Londoner living in Valparaiso, and is a certified sommelier. So he is especially good for native English speakers, though he is also fluent in Spanish. Michael has a wealth of knowledge about Chilean wine and cuisine and provided very useful insights throughout the tour. We went to three of the premier wineries in the Casablanca Valley, receiving tastings and behind-the-scenes tours at each. We had lunch at Macerado Restaurant, and it was probably the best meal we had during our time in Chile. We wrapped up with a mini tour of Valparaiso and ended at an excellent local wine shop. If we hadn't filled our suitcases during the tour, we would have bought more! I should note, however, that there was no pressure to buy anything at any point. It was just a great tour for the love of wine and food. In sum, I highly recommend Michael and Wine Tours Valparaiso for anyone looking to tour Chile's various wine regions. We will certainly ring him up again when we return.

Then, in the afternoon, I went to the Costanera Center and took the elevator up to the Sky Costanera observation deck. The view was incredible. I saw the entire city, the Andes Mountains, and the sunset from above. The ticket was a bit expensive, but it was worth it for the experience. I stayed there for a while, took photos, and admired the scenery. Later, I had dinner in a nearby restaurant and returned to my hotel. During my trip, I also visited other places, but seeing Santiago from the Sky Costanera was definitely one of the highlights. I stayed in the city for three days before returning home.

review_text: As far as free waking torus go this one was quite large, initially divided into English and Spanish speakers. The English group led by the energetic Valentina had well over twenty people walking sometimes in single file through crowded streets trying to find a patch of shade to stop. It is a long tour in the hot sun so bring a hat and even wear long sleeves as there is little shade en route. There is a stop around halfway to grab a quick snack in a recommended cafe. This could have been better managed as we later discovered there were other interesting options including a famous ice cream parlor just around the corner that we didn’t have time to stop in after the lunch break. A quick mention of other options would be been appreciated . We also discovered a great coffee spot nearby called Bloom Specialty coffee. Otherwise it is a whirlwind tour of Santiago districts, just scratching the surface of politics and history but whetting the appetite to encourage you to explore further another day.

review_text: Private Santiago City Half Day Tour by MTO Monday, 3/2/20: Santiago, Chile Today, we embarked upon a half-day private city tour of Santiago, the capital of Chile. We were picked up at 9:00 am by Maurcio, who navigated and Jania, who provided city highlights. This was definitely a great way to see the city in a safe and efficient manner. We made several stops for short walks and photo opportunities. We drove through the area where most of the demonstrations are held. Plaza Baquedano, also known as Plaza Italia, was built in 1928, and the features the General Manuel Baquedano monument created by Chilean sculptor Virgínio Arias. We passed the Central Market (Mercado Central), famous for multiple seafood dining options, and fresh seafood, sold at a number of stalls. We stopped at the Plaza de Armas, Santiago’s main square in the historical area. Considered “Kilometer Zero,” Plaza de Armas is the centerpiece of Santiago’s square grid pattern, and the point where distances are measured between other cities in Chile. Designed by Pedro de Gamboa, the Cabildo, or Town Hall House (now the Municipality of Santiago), the Governors’ House (now the Central Post Office), the Real Audiencia or Royal Courthouse (now the National History Museum), and the Iglesia Mayor, or Main Church (now the Metropolitan Cathedral) frame the square. There is a statue in honor of Don Pedro de Valdivia, and the contemporary STGO art installation. We walked through Plaza Montt Varas, also called Plaza de la Justicia, and viewed the lovely Palacio de los Tribunales de Justicia de Santiago (Courts of Justice Palace of Santiago), where the Chilean Supreme Court hears cases. There are intricate carvings along the roofline depicting the laws of Chile. Two lawyers, Manuel Montt, and Antonio Varas wrote some of Chile’s laws, are featured in a monument in the plaza. We entered the Chilean Museum of Precolombian Art, previously, colonial government’s Royal Customs House. The Fundacion Artesanias De Chile had a shop in the lobby with handmade goods from the Aymara people who live in Northern Chile. Their specialty is working with textiles, and I found a beautiful Alpaca scarf. We walked around the Palacio de La Moneda, previously home to the Republic of Chile’s president. Located between the streets Moneda (north), Morandé (east), the Alameda del Libertador Bernardo O'Higgins (south) and Teatinos (west), the building now houses governmental offices. The Plaza de la Constitución fronts the northern facade of the Palacio de la Moneda. We passed by the former National Congress Building (ex Congreso Nacional), the former home of the Chilean Congress. After Salvador Allende's socialist government was overthrown by dictator Augusto Pinochet's military coup d'état September 11, 1973, Congress moved to Valparaíso. We had a quick stop to view the Bellas Artes Museum (National Museum of Fine Arts), which is across from one of Santiago’s lovely city parks. There are two beautiful hills in Santiago with extraordinary views, Cerro Santa Lucia, and Cerro San Cristobal. Once a military look-out, Cerro Santa Lucia is accessed by a winding narrow road. A favorite of walkers and bicyclists, this is a beautiful park setting with a variety of foliage. Some areas are no longer accessible secondary to earthquake damage. Now an event center, the Castillo Hidalgo is close to the top. Unfortunately, the views were almost totally obscured by heavy smog. The Andes, while in the distance were mere faint shadows. On the other hand, the second hill, Cerro San Cristobal, was initially designed as a recreational park. There are two major ways to get up the hill, by cable car and by funicular. Unfortunately, today, both were out of operation, so we went up by car. There are two public swimming pools, the National Zoo, and lots of space for runners, walkers and hikers. Ascending a path with several concrete crosses depicting paintings of Christ, a steep set of stairs leads to the Sanctuary of the Immaculate Conception. There is an outdoor amphitheater with an altar for celebrating mass and at the summit a very large statue of the Virgin Mary overlooks the valley. On a clear day, the views would be amazing, but sadly, the smog obscured the landscape. Review of: Private Santiago City Half Day Tour Dear Julie, First of all, thank you very much for your comment. We are very happy to know that you enjoyed your experience with us and that you remember so much from all the places that you visited with us. We will pass on your comment to Mauricio and Jania. It is always very important for us and our guides to know that you enjoy and cherish every moment of your tour. It would be a pleasure for us to welcome you all again in the near future. Best regards, Maria from Mtotour

review_text: Took a 2D1N Salar de Uyuni tour with this company, which partnered with Cordillera Traveller to pool tour groups. First of all, if you are English speaking and pay for an English guide, please check whether the other members of the tour are Bolivian/Latin American. If possible, try to go with groups that are majority foreigner. I got a few lines of English every time we stopped and 85% of the explanations/scenery descriptions were in Spanish in the car. Not a huge problem but not what I paid a premium for. The guide was friendly and spoke good English. The guide had no experience/understanding of altitude sickness. I fell quite ill near the green lake on day 2. The guide told me to just wait it out while taking his time taking photos with other members of the tour group. When pressed about it, he told me he didn't really know how to deal with it and that we would be descending in 2hrs anyway. The guide finished the tour 2hrs late and had to rush the last part (tour of San Cristobal) due to poor time management. The guide was ill prepared and ran out of gas halfway. We had to drive around a small town asking 4 different groups of people till we found someone willing to sell gas. If we were far away from a town when this happened it would have been even more disastrous.

review_text: If you ever go to Arica, this museum is a must. Located after a short trip from Arica. This museum and the town itself is worth to be discovered. The surroundings are very calm as San Miguel de Azapa is a quiet town. In the museum you can know about the historical evolution of the region, and learn about the oldest mummies ever found in the whole world. The museum is clearly indicated, although there isn't enough information in English. In the outside there's a park with objects found from the time when the Indians lived there. There's also a museum about the importance of the olive trees in the valley, as well as banana trees outside, something quite unique in Chile. It is totally worth the experience!

review_text: My husband and I visited Chile in 2012 and 2013. We had the opportunity to take several of the trips with the owners of On The Road Patagonia. I can not recommend them enough. Everything was easy, informative, (bilingual) and a lot of fun! During your stay in Punta Arenas I would, of course, NOT miss the penguins tour. We visited the colony at Seno Otway and we were not disappointed. There are paths and viewing areas in the reserve and as you walk along you get a chance to get up close and watch these amazing creatures. Dress warm!! We also did the day hike in the Reserva with On the Road Patagonia which was a nice way to spend a half day in nature right outside of the city. Later in the day they took us to have the most delicious crab empanadas we have ever tasted. On our last day we took the tour to the Historical Fort Bulnes along the southern coast highway and it was amazingly beautiful. We hiked along the shoreline with one of the guides. It was truly a magical place. The guide was wonderful and it was obvious she enjoyed what she was doing as much as we enjoyed being with her. The year before we visited Torres Del Paine and trekked with the guides from On the Road Patagonia. WOW is all I can say. It is so beautiful and the hiking/trekking was challenging but doable and so much fun. If you have the time I would take the W circuit. On the Road Patagonia can arrange everything for you, which I highly recommend because it might be hard to figure out all of the details on your own. There is the option of camping or bunking in Refugios along the route. The owner of On the Road Patagonia is from the Patagonia and previously worked in Torres del Paine which we found extremely helpful. He is very accommodating and supportive of your needs.

review_text: Ok. Apparently by the title this seems to be one of my favourite places. And it is, indeed. But why? What makes Parque Forestal so great? Well...keep on reading folks. And you will soon realize why this is by far one of the best places to go if you ever have the chance to visit Santiago. First of all, let's locate ourselves here. Parque forestal, it's really close to Bellas Artes metro station (5 min walk). So, you go there and you find this huge park that goes along Costanera street, where you can find one of the most important museums in Santiago. Bellas Artes museum. The entrance here is free!!... yes, FREE!. (oh, and it's closed on Monday's). You can find different expositions and also enjoy from the amazing architecture it has. On the other side of the museum, you can finde the MAC, Where you can appreciate comtemporary and modern art and different monthly expositions too. -If you want to appreciate a truly unique piece, and aren't really in a "museum mood", you can admire de front part of the museum and the Bottero Horse (a sculpture right outside of the museum)- So, don't you already think it's cool enough? OK, let me keep trying to convince you haha. If you cross the street (Ismael Valdés Vergara), walking south, you get to Monjitas St. Here, you can find Bars, Restaurants, Coffe shops (specially in Mosqueto st., which crosses monjita's street, no need to walk extra miles). Convinced yet? If not, just give it a chance, I promise you, you won't regret it.

review_text: Our guide from HecTourService picked 6 of us up from our hotel in Santiago and drove us to Valparaiso. The van was immaculate and we felt in very good hands with our guide/driver. On the way to Valparaiso our guide asked us if we would like to make a stop to try his favorite place for empanadas. This "place" was a private home of a woman who supplies empanadas for many of the restaurants in the surrounding area. They were the best empanadas we had on our 7 week adventure in South America, we really appreciated this personal touch. Valparaiso is a colorful and quaint port town with unique and embracing street art, and an interesting history. Our guide was very engaging, knowledgeable and knew where all the points of interest were. He directed us to a restaurant where we had a delicious lunch with gorgeous views. Not once during the tour did he look at his watch or hurry us along, his priority was to make sure we were enjoying ourselves. Without our guide we would have burned a lot of time trying to find the different points of interest, likely missing many. Maybe more importantly he maneuvered us through the very hilly and windy street, that were wide enough to comfortable fit one car at a time, but allowed two. I highly recommend HecTour Service and would use them again if ever in the area in the future.

review_text: Rambling, creative architecture, quirky collections of world art, and a glimpse into the private life of a passionate poet, all with a stunning ocean view: that's how I'd describe our visit to Pablo Neruda's home at Isla Negra. It is the most intact of Nerdua's three homes in Chile, much of his personal property remains intact here as opposed to his other two homes, one in Santiago, the other in Valparaiso. I have been a fan of Neruda's sensuous poems ever since I stumbled upon them in a bookshop 35 years ago, and this tour gave me an idea of what he must have been like, and a better appreciation for his life as a world traveler, diplomat and favorite son of Chile. Plus he had excellent taste in objects d'arte! The guide did not discuss much of his life or writings and would have given a rather perfunctory tour had it not been for lively questions coming from our interested group. But the guide did have answers, showing that she actually was fairly well-versed in her subject matter and just needed a little prodding. If you have the time and any interest in Pablo Neruda, who is probably the greatest poet of our times, I highly recommend a visit to Isla Negra.

review_text: We booked 3 tours with the agency and had problems with 2 of them, 66%. Maybe this is the likelihood that you will be upset if you book a tour with them. The first one, Alyan, was incredible, however, the next day we had made a reservation for concha y toro, and amazingly, when we got there, our van and another one from we love Chile, had no reservation, that is, more or less 30 people were left without entering. They even relocated us to another winery, however, what we bought was concha y toro, and unfortunately we returned to Chile without seeing it. On the last tour, Vale Experience, when we got into the van, there were only two seats available, which didn't even fit our legs (photos below) and anyone who knows knows that going through the curves of Chile with poor accommodation is complicated. Anyway, we spoke to several Brazilians who booked tours with other agencies, and no one had any problems. My opinion is that what they sell on Instagram is not compatible with what they deliver. Furthermore, upon arriving in Santiago we went to the agency to make the rest of the payment and were very unwelcome. review_text: La Bicicleta Verde were super organized, they emailed several time prior to pick up day with confirmations, which made pick-up from my hotel seamless. We scooted out to the countryside in a nice modern van and drew up at a local family-run restaurant where were treated to an (included) breakfast of coffee and empanadas. You then jump on their bikes, taking a leisurely and pretty flat cycle out amongst the beauty of the local vineyards set against the dramatic backdrop of the Andes. All the way along our guide delivered timely snippets of information in a charming and funny manner. We saw a variety of vineyards under different management systems, saw inside the processing and bottling plants and heard a lot of history and cultural information along the way. The final leg of the tour gave us a chance to check out a free museum of local art and historical artifacts, then on to the Santa Rita vineyard where we were taken down into their historic cellar for a movie on the history of the vineyard (it actually does have a story, I will not spoil it for you if you don’t know it). Another charming and funny guide then led a wine tasting accompanies by cheese and bikkies. You can then shop for wines and local delicacies, before heading back to the little restaurant for lunch which was also nice. I loved this day and thought the company delivered it to a T. The two guides Juan and Pablo were lovely, knowledgable and personable. Our driver didn’t speak much English but was a lovely friendly gent as well. If I was there for longer I would have definitely have done more of this companies tours. I had a great experience and have already recommended to friends who are heading to Santiago soon. review_text: We were a group of 4 from Australia and booked the one day trip to Valparaiso and had Jana as our very accomplished guide. We stopped at the local fish markets by the sea and were greeted by loads of sea lions and pelicans awaiting fish scraps. Valparaiso is a port town, full of very creative street art and brightly coloured buildings so best explored on foot. It was valuable to have a guide such as Jana take us up into the hilly streets and stairs which showcased these best. We were taken to a local non tourist restaurant and Jana ordered a selection of seafood dishes for us which were fresh and tasty. On the way back to Santiago, we stopped at Emiliana Organic Vineyard which has some resident alpacas and beautiful and peaceful surroundings. We had a young and talented winemaker take us through the whites and reds which were excellent and well priced. It was a fabulous day and Jana looked after us very well. We all highly recommend Turismo Flecha Extrema and look forward to further tours particularly the horse riding and hot springs tours, on our next visit.

review_text: First impressions always count and when we first glimpsed this gorgeous lake it was the sheer size and volume of water that took us by surprise. In fact it reminded us of an inland sea or perhaps of the Lakes district in Italy albeit much, much larger! That description only fits so far because as we drove the entire lake circuit the iconic Osorno Volcano makes its presence felt just about everywhere you look. We have seen Mt Fuji with its lake however; Llanquihue has the most stunning surroundings including a backdrop of rolling farmlands and cute little towns before the rise of the Andes on the far eastern side of this lake. Our drive started in Puerto Varas, the most touristy town on the lake then continued on a brief freeway that evens out to a less busy road to the German heritage town of Fruitillar. Here the quietly lapping water beckons summer holiday makers and has a bit of a resort feel - without the high rises! The drive veers away from the lake here enroute to Puerto Octay and where the roads get a little bumpy. It was worth it though as there is a magnificent lookout here the shows the higher northern aspect of the lake. Although this town is small, it has a Bavarian flair surrounded by dairy fields. As we got closer to Ensenada the forests appeared very close to the lakeshore.Further on you can divert to Osorno National Park or continue along the main route of the lake.Once again we were back in the heart of the tourist throng amongst the roadside souvenir stalls and a couple of interesting restaurants. We allowed several hours to include the lake circuit, the National Park and some time at each well-known town or area along the drive. However, we had to slow down on the road we used between Frutillar and Puerto Octay - inland slightly through dairy farms. Nonetheless, it’s a spectacular way to see Llanquihue particularly if it’s a fine day. Enjoy your experience!

review_text: We went on a self-drive trip up here. It is recommended to go here in the morning if driving yourself as after 1pm the tourist buses generally come in for afternoon and evening tours and the lake gets swamped with people. In the morning it is fairly quiet and limited number of people. The lake itself is wondrous, and not something I had experienced ever before. As one walks into the water the initial feeling is just that the water is very cold and not much else. After wading through knee deep and waist deep water for about 40-50m one finally gets to the deep part of the lake where the bottom falls off. This is where the magic happens! Once you garner the courage to take plunge into the deep you realise how much more buoyant the salty water is from normal fresh water or even sea water. The water just pushes you right up to the surface and without even trying one can float easily on the surface. It is just a very other worldly feeling. It is hard to spend too much time in the water as it is really very cold but every moment is enjoyable. There is some cold water showers near the parking with fresh water to take a quick shower before leaving.

review_text: We enjoyed a fairly quick exit from the ship and were met by Marilyn and our driver Mr. Sammy. Marilyn is a young mother of three girls who is training to be a teacher of high school English. Her grammar is very good and her vocabulary is building. She had no trouble sharing her beautiful home area with us. The original settlementwas named for the Chilean President at that time, Manuel Montt and dates back to 1853, when Vincente Perez Rosales and a group of intrepid German immigrants decided to colonize the densely forested region around Lake Llanquihue. When train service arrived in the early 29th century the city really took off and became a popular stop off for travelers between Magallnes and Chiloe. The city was United, and then rebuilt after the 1960 earthquake. It is more recently know for it's salmon, but they are farmed Atlantic Salmon. The area was settled by Germans and has a very different flavor from all our ports so far. The houses have the German touch and are small but two stories which make for easier heating. As we travelled to Puerto Vargas we saw a change as this area is very much a resort area and the houses are more sprawling and larger properties. There are many farms along the way. The agriculture is very important here as is the fishing industry. There is lots of fruit as well as fields of corn. The apples are tiny but very sweet and there is a berry called the Macca? Which is sort of like a blue berry and used in lot of baking. We could see the devastation from the volcano eruption last year. The ash sits very deep along the sides of the roads in some places and only a drift in others. The park Vincente Perez Rosales is free right now and was not before. Many things described to us was defined as before or after the eruptions. We enjoyed our walk to see the falls, which are really Rapids. We all had a laugh later as we all thought we heard the guide say we would next be going to see the rabbits. The rapids are impressive as a large volume of water is channeled into a very narrow spillway and has dug it's way very deeply into the ground. We then drove along the river to the All Saints Lake. Very pretty, but not for swimming. It was tempting, but we refrained from getting in the water. Our day then took us to a little mom and pop place where we enjoyed some really good homemade empanadas right out of the oven. Mr. Sammy and Marilyn joined us for lunch. The trip was not over. Another short walk along a nature trail which was a relaxing way to let our lunch settle. We ended our day in the resort area, shopping the goal for some and a walk along the waterfront for us. We booked a van for six which was perfect. We managed to avoid most of the big buses and had an amazing day.

review_text: Katenke is a small operator run by Christian Restepo Ruiz out of Cochrane. He has developed this concept of snorkling down the Cochrane river for 3.5 km and thus seeing things from a totally different perspective. The time in the 8 C cold water lasts about 1½ hour and on the way you see many plants, colorful roots, rocks, gravel, sand, lots of healthy trout and, unfortunately, also some garbage. Christian and his team try to keep the waters free of trash by once a month cleaning up but even here, along the clean and untouched Carretera Austral, people seem to miss good habits when it comes to trash. In spite of the cold, glacial water you are not cold as you are equipped with double thick wetsuits with hoods, goggles, flippers, shoes and gloves. The float takes you through narrow passages as well as open, broad passages of the river and is very varied. Christian and his assistant, Frencisco, all the time take good care of you, give thorough instructions before the dive and make up the head and tail of the procession of floaters. If you have snorkled before there are ample possibilities to dive down as the depth of water varies between 1-6 meters. If you are looking for a different and affordable experience on your way down the Carretera Austral this event is strongly recommended,

review_text: As a professional bird guide and bird photographer who leads birding tours in the US and Canada, I highly recommend Albatross Birding and Nature Tours. My wife and I took a pelagic trip with them from Valparaíso on December 11, 2021, and everything went perfectly. The folks in the booking office spoke excellent English, they responded to emails very promptly, and their instructions on where to park and how find the group were crystal clear. The boat was basic but very sturdy, and our keen-eyed guide shouted out the birds as they appeared. Importantly, he knew the bird names in Spanish and English. As for the birding, it was SPECTACULAR. I've taken over 70 pelagic trips between California, North Carolina, Florida, New York, Massachusetts, and New Zealand, and this was one of my best offshore experiences. Chum brought the birds close to the boat, and we had amazing looks at Buller's, Salvin's, Black-browed, Royal, and Chatham Albatrosses. Though farther away, Masatierra and Juan Fernandez Petrel also made quick passes. White-chinned Petrels and Pink-footed Shearwaters were everywhere, and we had Chilean Skuas and Peruvian Diving-Petrels at multiple points on our trip. If you go pelagic birding with Albatross, then bring your camera because the photographic opportunities were fantastic.

review_text: I was lucky to stay at Awasi so I was able to do a private tour instead of a bus group tour. The departure time is around 5:30 - 6. However you need to be there by 8 am as by 9, it gets too hot and the steam dissipates. On the way, do note the flamingoes at the marshy area just before the Machuca River. There are three varieties and it was a beautiful sight to see them in flight. Then the Machuca itself is beautiful, plenty of birds, coots, ducks etc. The coots actually nest in the river (the nest is made from reeds which are used to feed the chicks). Then you reach Tatio itself. It should be around -5 degrees C at that time of the morning so dress for it. There is also a public pool from the hot spring but I did not try it. Around the area more fauna of interest include fox, rabbit, guanaco, alpaca, so keep your eyes open. We had breakfast next to our pickup and then were back in San Pedro around 11:30.
